For $u,v\in\mathbb C^3$, extend the real Euclidean dot and right-handed cross products complex-bilinearly, with coordinate formulas
$$u\cdot v:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jv_j,\qquad u\times v:=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1).$$
The dot product in these formulas uses no complex conjugation; it differs from the Hermitian product $\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{u_j}v_j$. Write $\|z\|_H:=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle_H}$ for the associated nonnegative norm on $\mathbb C^3$.

Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot n=1\}$ with the smooth structure given by the six graph charts solving $n_j=\pm\sqrt{1-\sum_{k\ne j}n_k^2}$ on the hemispheres $\pm n_j>0$. Orient it outward using the ordered spatial basis $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its tangent plane is $T_nS^2=\{X\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot X=0\}$. Physically, $n=k/|k|$ for a nonzero spatial wavevector $k$ in the SI Fourier description, where $k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; hence $n$ is dimensionless and the radial magnitude is discarded. For $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$, set $C_nz:=i\,n\times z$, $P_T(n)z:=z-n(n\cdot z)$, and $P_\sigma(n):=\tfrac12(P_T(n)+\sigma C_n)$ on $\mathbb C^3$. Define the helicity fibre $L_\sigma(n):=\operatorname{range}P_\sigma(n)$ and the total space $L_\sigma:=\{(n,z):n\in S^2,\ z\in L_\sigma(n)\}$, projected to $S^2$ by $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

For an open set $U\subseteq S^2$, a unit frame of $L_\sigma$ over $U$ is a smooth map $v:U\to\mathbb C^3$ such that $v(n)\in L_\sigma(n)$ and $\langle v(n),v(n)\rangle_H=1$ for every $n\in U$. Since each fibre is a complex line, this vector spans that fibre. A local unit frame is such a map on an open neighborhood in $S^2$; a global unit frame is one defined on all of $S^2$.

Fibrewise addition and scalar multiplication are inherited from $\mathbb C^3$. A unit frame $v$ gives the local trivialization $(n,a)\mapsto(n,a v(n))$ from $U\times\mathbb C$ to $L_\sigma|_U$, with inverse $(n,z)\mapsto(n,\langle v(n),z\rangle_H)$. The construction in the Proof supplies such a frame near every $n$, so $L_\sigma$ is a smooth rank-one complex vector subbundle of the product bundle $S^2\times\mathbb C^3\to S^2$, whose projection is $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

On a spherical chart with $0<\theta<\pi$ and a smooth longitude branch $\phi$, write $n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$, $e_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\sin\phi,-\sin\theta)$, and $e_\phi=(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi,0)$. The local unit helicity frame is $v_\sigma:=(e_\theta+i\sigma e_\phi)/\sqrt2$. For any unit frame $v$ over an open set $U$, write $v^\dagger d v:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{v_j}\,d v_j$, where $d v_j$ is the exterior derivative of its $j$th component. Define its Berry connection one-form by $A:=i v^\dagger d v$. A smooth phase change $v'=e^{i\chi}v$, with real smooth $\chi$, changes this local form to $A'=A-d\chi$. The local Berry curvature is the real two-form $F:=dA$ on $U$; no global gluing assertion is made here.

For $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, let $n:=k/|k|$ and let the complex
transverse fibre be
$T_k:=\{v\in\mathbb C^3:\sum_j k_jv_j=0\}$. On $\mathbb C^3$ define
$C(k)v:=i\,n\times v$ and
$P_T(k)v:=v-n\sum_j n_jv_j$. Define
$P_\sigma(k):=\tfrac12(P_T(k)+\sigma C(k))$ for $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$.
Use the Hermitian product
$\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j$. Then $P_T(k)$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $T_k$; $C(k)$ is Hermitian, vanishes on the
longitudinal line, and satisfies $C(k)^2=P_T(k)$. The restrictions of
$P_{+1}(k)$ and $P_{-1}(k)$ to $T_k$ are orthogonal rank-one projections with
sum $P_T(k)$. Their ranges are the two helicity eigenspaces, with eigenvalues
$+1$ and $-1$ for $C(k)$.

Fix $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$ and let $L_\sigma(n)$ be the range of the helicity projector $P_\sigma(n)$ over the outward-oriented unit sphere $S^2$. On an angular chart with $0<\theta<\pi$ and a smooth longitude branch $\phi$, use $v_\sigma=(e_\theta+i\sigma e_\phi)/\sqrt2$ and the connection convention $A_\sigma=i v_\sigma^\dagger d v_\sigma$. The spherical frame has Berry one-form $A_\sigma=\sigma\cos\theta\,d\phi$ and curvature $F_\sigma=dA_\sigma=-\sigma\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. If $\omega_{S^2,n}(X,Y):=n\cdot(X\times Y)$ is the outward area form for $X,Y\in T_nS^2$, then this curvature extends smoothly to the whole sphere as $F_\sigma=-\sigma\omega_{S^2}$. Write $\int_{S^2}$ for the outward-oriented integral, evaluated as the sum over the eight radially projected octant triangles described in the Proof. Its total flux is $\int_{S^2}F_\sigma=-4\pi\sigma$, so the flux divided by $2\pi$ is $-2\sigma$ in this convention. The line bundle has no globally smooth unit frame.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

derivations.claim: For $z\in L_\sigma(n)$, [F2] gives $n\cdot z=0$ and $n\times z=-i\sigma z$. The defining formula therefore reduces to $R_{n,\alpha}z=(\cos\alpha-i\sigma\sin\alpha)z=e^{-i\sigma\alpha}z$. The phase is unchanged when $\alpha$ is increased by $2\pi$ because $\sigma$ is an integer, and addition of angles multiplies phases, proving it is the stated character.

Choose a real unit vector $u\perp n$ and put $v=n\times u$. The real cross-product identities give $|v|=1$, $u\cdot v=0$, and $n\times v=-u$, so $(u,v,n)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis. In this basis the real rotation formula has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha&0\\ \sin\alpha&\cos\alpha&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which is orthogonal with determinant one. Thus $R_{n,\alpha}$ is proper.

Write a section on one chart as $s(t)=a(t)v_j(\gamma(t))$. Since $P_\sigma$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by the unit vector $v_j$, the projected derivative is $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}s=(\dot a+a\,v_j^\dagger\dot v_j)v_j=(\dot a-iA_j(\dot\gamma)a)v_j$. Thus $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}s=0$ is the scalar ODE $\dot a=iA_j(\dot\gamma)a$, whose solution across that subpath multiplies $a$ by $\exp(i\int A_j)$. At an internal join, equality of the section on both frames gives $a_{j+1}v_{j+1}=a_jv_j$, hence $a_{j+1}=g_j^{-1}a_j$. At the end, $v_m(\gamma(1))=g_mv_1(\gamma(0))$ converts the final coefficient to $g_ma_m$ in the starting frame. Multiplying these scalar factors gives the formula in the Statement.

If a frame on subpath $j$ is changed to $v'_j=h_jv_j$ with $h_j$ smooth and $U(1)$-valued, the local connection changes by $A'_j=A_j+i h_j^{-1}dh_j$ (locally $h_j=e^{i\chi_j}$ this is $A_j-d\chi_j$). The segment exponential acquires the endpoint ratio $h_j(t_j)^{-1}h_j(t_{j-1})$; the adjacent transition factors change by the inverse endpoint ratios. These factors cancel at every internal join and at the identified loop endpoint. Thus the product formula is independent of the chosen local frames; no single global $A$ is assumed.

For the Stokes clause, one frame is defined on the open set containing the image of $\Sigma$. By the line-integral definition and the affine reparametrizations in $c_\gamma$, $\int_{c_\gamma}A=\oint_\gamma A$. Since $\partial\Sigma=c_\gamma$, the cited Stokes theorem [F4] gives $\int_\Sigma dA=\int_{\partial\Sigma}A=\int_{c_\gamma}A$. The local curvature is $F_\sigma=dA$ by [F3], so exponentiation gives $\mathrm{Hol}_\gamma=\exp(i\int_\Sigma F_\sigma)$. For paths or surfaces requiring more than one patch, the transition factors in step 2.1 are part of the holonomy; a bare integral of a nonexistent global one-form is not asserted.

and its linearized Maxwell residuals are
$$df,\qquad d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F),\qquad \delta(\star\mathcal F):=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0}\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon.$$
Here $g_\epsilon=g+\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $\mathcal F_\epsilon=\mathcal F+\epsilon f+O(\epsilon^2)$ are smooth local families on the fixed domain, with dimensionless parameter $\epsilon$. The derivatives are the coordinatewise derivatives of these smooth finite-jet operators; the chain rule makes them depend only on $(h,f)$, not on the higher-order parts of the chosen families. The **linearized electrovacuum system** is the homogeneous system $\delta E_{(g,\mathcal F)}[h,f]=0$, $df=0$, and $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$.

Let $\Phi_\epsilon:V	o W$ be an orientation-preserving local flow map. Define its pulled-back connection by $(\Phi_\epsilon^*
abla)_XY:=\Phi_{\epsilon*}^{-1}(
abla_{\Phi_{\epsilon*}X}\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y)$. The coordinate Lie-bracket identity in [F3] and the chain rule give $[\Phi_{\epsilon*}X,\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y]=\Phi_{\epsilon*}[X,Y]$, so this connection is torsion-free. For vector fields $X,Y,Z$, differentiating $(\Phi_\epsilon^*g)(Y,Z)=g(\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y,\Phi_{\epsilon*}Z)\circ\Phi_\epsilon$ and using $
abla g=0$ shows it is compatible with $\Phi_\epsilon^*g$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies it with $
abla^{\Phi_\epsilon^*g}$. Applying this definition twice in the curvature formula and using the same bracket identity gives $R[\Phi_\epsilon^*g](X,Y)Z=\Phi_{\epsilon*}^{-1}(R[g](\Phi_{\epsilon*}X,\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y)\Phi_{\epsilon*}Z)$; the trace defining Ricci is unchanged under conjugation by $D\Phi_\epsilon$, hence $\operatorname{Ric}[\Phi_\epsilon^*g]=\Phi_\epsilon^*\operatorname{Ric}[g]$. The formula for $Q$ uses only tensor products, the metric inverse and contractions; $(\Phi_\epsilon^*g)^{-1}(\Phi_\epsilon^*\alpha,\Phi_\epsilon^* eta)=\Phi_\epsilon^*(g^{-1}(\alpha, eta))$ by the inverse linear map, so $Q(\Phi_\epsilon^*g,\Phi_\epsilon^*\mathcal F)=\Phi_\epsilon^*Q(g,\mathcal F)$. In the defining Hodge identity, pullback commutes with alternating tensor evaluation and the inverse-metric pairing; it also carries $\mathrm{vol}_g$ to $\mathrm{vol}_{\Phi_\epsilon^*g}$ because the flow preserves orientation and the volume density transforms by the Jacobian determinant. Uniqueness of the Hodge map therefore gives $\star_{\Phi_\epsilon^*g}\Phi_\epsilon^*\mathcal F=\Phi_\epsilon^*(\star_g\mathcal F)$. Finally, write a $k$-form as $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I dx^I$. By [F4], $d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I$. The chain rule gives the terms where a derivative hits $\omega_I$; terms where it hits a coordinate derivative of $\Phi_\epsilon$ cancel in pairs because second partial derivatives commute while the exterior product is alternating. Hence $d\Phi_\epsilon^*\omega=\Phi_\epsilon^*d\omega$. Thus every exact residual of the pulled-back pair is the pullback of the corresponding zero residual.

For a smooth exact family $(g_\lambda,\mathcal F_\lambda)$ on a common open set, each of its three residuals in [F1] is identically zero as a smooth function of $(\lambda,x)$. Differentiating in $\lambda$ commutes with the finite coordinate derivatives and contractions in those residuals, so their derivatives at any $\lambda_0$ are exactly the linearized residuals of $(\partial_\lambda g,\partial_\lambda\mathcal F)|_{\lambda_0}$ and vanish.

Differentiating the residual identities of step 1.1 at $\epsilon=0$ gives zero linearized metric and Maxwell residuals; in the Hodge residual the varied tensor is the explicit $\delta(\star\mathcal F)$ of [F5]. By the definition of the Lie derivative through the local flow, the derivatives of the pulled-back fields are precisely $(\dot\Phi_0^*g,\dot\Phi_0^*\mathcal F)$, so this is the asserted pure-gauge solution.

The RN and KN data of [F6] are smooth in their displayed parameters on any fixed exterior domain satisfying the relevant strict chart inequalities. Restricting the parameter interval around the chosen values if necessary preserves those inequalities on the common domain. Both verification results establish the exact equations with $\Lambda=0$, so step 1.2 applies to each such parameter derivative in that fixed sector. The parameter derivatives are stationary because the displayed metric and field coefficients are independent of $x^0$. No inference is made that an arbitrary linearized solution lies on one of these families.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix such a background on $U$. A **linearized perturbation** is a pair $(h,f)$ consisting of a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $h$ and a smooth real two-form $f$ on $U$. Its linearized metric residual is
$$\delta E_{(g,\mathcal F)}[h,f]:=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0}\bigl(\operatorname{Ric}[g_\epsilon]-\Lambda g_\epsilon-2Q(g_\epsilon,\mathcal F_\epsilon)\bigr),$$
and its linearized Maxwell residuals are
$$df,\qquad d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F),\qquad \delta(\star\mathcal F):=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0}\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon.$$
Here $g_\epsilon=g+\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $\mathcal F_\epsilon=\mathcal F+\epsilon f+O(\epsilon^2)$ are smooth local families on the fixed domain, with dimensionless parameter $\epsilon$. The derivatives are the coordinatewise derivatives of these smooth finite-jet operators; the chain rule makes them depend only on $(h,f)$, not on the higher-order parts of the chosen families. The **linearized electrovacuum system** is the homogeneous system $\delta E_{(g,\mathcal F)}[h,f]=0$, $df=0$, and $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$.

Let $g_\epsilon=g+\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2)$ be a smooth variation of an oriented Lorentzian metric on a four-manifold, and let $\omega_\epsilon=\omega+\epsilon\tau+O(\epsilon^2)$ be a smooth variation of a $k$-form, $0\le k\le4$. Define $h_a{}^b:=g^{bc}h_{ac}$, $\operatorname{tr}_g h:=g^{ab}h_{ab}$, and
$$\bigl(h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega\bigr)_{a_1\ldots a_k}:=\sum_{j=1}^k h_{a_j}{}^b\omega_{a_1\ldots a_{j-1}b a_{j+1}\ldots a_k},$$
with $h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega:=0$ for $k=0$. Then
$$\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_0\star_{g_\epsilon}\omega_\epsilon=\star_g\left(\tau+\frac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\omega-h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega\right).$$
In particular, for the geometric background $\mathcal F$ and perturbation $f$ of [[def-emg-fx-linearized-electrovac]],
$$\delta(\star\mathcal F)=\star_g\left(f+\frac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\mathcal F-h^\sharp\!\cdot\mathcal F\right).$$
If $(h,f)$ satisfies the linearized Maxwell equation, then $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$; this last condition is exactly the derivative of $d(\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon)=0$, not a consequence of the variation formula alone.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited from the smooth principal-connection convention. Fix an oriented, time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N,o)$ and a fixed normalized $U(1)$ connection sector as in the fixed-topology affine-sector result. Its connection variations are global smooth real one-forms $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^1(M)$, with components of unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ in length-coordinate charts. Length-coordinate charts use metre-valued coordinates, with $x^0=ct_{\mathrm{sec}}$ when time is recorded in seconds; $c$ is a coordinate unit-conversion scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, with no numerical measured value or physical role asserted. Impose the fixed-background Maxwell operator equations $d\star_g d\alpha=0$ and $d\star_g d\beta=0$, where $\star_g$ is the oriented Lorentzian Hodge map of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Define the real three-form

$$\omega_g(\alpha,\beta):=\alpha\wedge\star_g d\beta-\beta\wedge\star_g d\alpha.$$

Let $\iota_\Sigma:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$ be an oriented smooth embedding of a possibly noncompact three-dimensional manifold, and require the induced metric $\gamma:=\iota_\Sigma^*g$ to be positive definite. Its oriented Riemannian volume form is the nowhere-vanishing three-form $\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$ whose expression in each positively oriented chart $y=(y^1,y^2,y^3)$ is $\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{ij})}\,dy^1\wedge dy^2\wedge dy^3$. Let $\mu_\gamma$ be the positive smooth density measure with coordinate expression $d\mu_\gamma=\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{ij})}\,d^3y$. The density-measure integration supplier listed below gives the chart-independent measure and integral; for a real $L^1(\mu_\gamma)$ function its signed integral is the finite difference of the integrals of its positive and negative parts, and its chart formula is absolutely convergent.

There is a unique smooth real function $u_{\alpha,\beta}$ on $\Sigma$ such that $\iota_\Sigma^*\omega_g(\alpha,\beta)=u_{\alpha,\beta}\,\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$. Define the pairing $\Omega_\Sigma(\alpha,\beta)$ precisely when $u_{\alpha,\beta}\in L^1(\Sigma,\mu_\gamma)$, meaning $\int_\Sigma|u_{\alpha,\beta}|\,d\mu_\gamma<\infty$, and then set $\Omega_\Sigma(\alpha,\beta):=\int_\Sigma u_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\mu_\gamma$. This absolute-integrability condition is the convergence convention on noncompact $\Sigma$ and makes the value independent of any exhaustion or ordering. In length coordinates on $\Sigma$, the coefficients of $d\alpha$ and $d\beta$ have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$, those of $\omega_g$ have units $\mathrm m^{-3}$, $u_{\alpha,\beta}$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}$, and $d\mu_\gamma$ has volume units $\mathrm m^3$; thus the normalized integral is dimensionless. Replacing normalized variations by physical-potential variations $\kappa_0\alpha$ and $\kappa_0\beta$ multiplies the current by $\kappa_0^2$; an action prefactor is not fixed here.

This is a mathematical fixed-metric Maxwell-block definition. The equations are imposed on the normalized connection variations. The item does not identify $\kappa_0d\alpha$ with the geometric-normalized electrovac field of the coupled Einstein–Maxwell equations, prescribe a conversion between those normalizations, include metric variations, or claim to define the full coupled covariant phase-space current.

derivations.claim: Applying the graded product rule to each term of [F1] gives $d\omega_g=d\alpha\wedge\star_g d\beta-\alpha\wedge d\star_g d\beta-d\beta\wedge\star_g d\alpha+\beta\wedge d\star_g d\alpha$. The first and third terms cancel because the two-form pairing in [F2] is symmetric, and the other two vanish by the stated equations. Hence $d\omega_g=0$.

Since $d^2\chi=0$ by [F2], the change in [F1] under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha+d\chi$ is exactly $d\chi\wedge\star_g d\beta$. On the other hand, $d(\chi\star_g d\beta)=d\chi\wedge\star_g d\beta+\chi\,d\star_g d\beta=d\chi\wedge\star_g d\beta$. The current change is therefore the exact three-form $d(\chi\star_g d\beta)$.

Integrating the exact change over a finite smooth singular three-chain $c$ and applying [F3] gives $\int_c d(\chi\star_g d\beta)=\int_{\partial c}\chi\star_g d\beta$. This is zero when $c$ is a cycle, while for a chain with boundary it is the displayed boundary flux.

Now let $\Sigma$ be noncompact, assume both current pairings in the Statement are defined, and choose a compact Borel exhaustion with finite-chain representatives as in the Statement. Write $\iota_\Sigma^*(\omega_g(\alpha+d\chi,\beta)-\omega_g(\alpha,\beta))=u\,\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$. The two current coefficients are in $L^1(\mu_\gamma)$, so their difference $u$ is also in $L^1(\mu_\gamma)$ by $|u|\leq |u_{\alpha+d\chi,\beta}|+|u_{\alpha,\beta}|$. Since $K_n\uparrow\Sigma$, both $\mathbf1_{K_n}u^+$ and $\mathbf1_{K_n}u^-$ increase pointwise to $u^+$ and $u^-$. Applying [F4] separately to these nonnegative functions and subtracting their finite limits gives $\int_{K_n}u\,d\mu_\gamma\to\int_\Sigma u\,d\mu_\gamma$. By the defining property of $c_n$ and [F3], $\int_{\partial c_n}\chi\star_g d\beta=\int_{c_n}d(\chi\star_g d\beta)=\int_{K_n}u\,d\mu_\gamma$. This proves the stated flux identity. For the fixed $\beta$, the shift vanishes exactly when the limiting flux is zero; on a specified test space this must hold for every allowed $\beta$ for the gauge direction to be degenerate. No falloff condition is inferred from the field equations alone.

$$g=-\left(e^{2\beta}\frac Vr-r^2\gamma_{AB}U^AU^B\right)du^2-2e^{2\beta}du\,dr-2r^2\gamma_{AB}U^Bdu\,dx^A+r^2\gamma_{AB}dx^A dx^B,$$

where $\beta,V,U^A,\gamma_{AB}$ are smooth, $\gamma_{AB}$ is positive definite, $\gamma^{AC}\gamma_{CB}=\delta^A_B$, and $\det(\gamma_{AB})=\det(q_{AB})$. Thus $u=\mathrm{constant}$ are outgoing null hypersurfaces, $r$ is the area radius, and $x^A$ are constant along their null generators. This Bondi gauge has $g_{rr}=g_{rA}=0$.

A **smooth Bondi expansion** is such an end with the differentiated uniform expansions

$$\gamma_{AB}=q_{AB}+\frac{C_{AB}(u,x)}r+\frac{P_{AB}(u,x)}{r^2}+O(r^{-3}),\qquad \beta=O(r^{-2}),\qquad U^A=\frac{U^A_{(2)}(u,x)}{r^2}+\frac{U^A_{(3)}(u,x)}{r^3}+O(r^{-4}),\qquad V=r-2m(u,x)+\frac{V_{(1)}(u,x)}r+O(r^{-2}).$$

Here $C_{AB}$, $P_{AB}$ and the displayed coefficients are smooth sphere fields on $I$; the determinant gauge imposes $q^{AB}C_{AB}=0$ and $q^{AB}P_{AB}=\tfrac12 C_{AB}C^{AB}$. For every compact $I'\subset I$, angular chart compact set, and derivative multi-index $\alpha$ of total order at most two, the partial derivatives of each $O(r^{-k})$ remainder obey $\partial_u^{\alpha_u}D^{\alpha_x}\partial_r^{\alpha_r}O(r^{-k})=O(r^{-k-\alpha_r})$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$. Define the **mass aspect** $m$ by the $r^{-1}$ coefficient in $V$, the **Bondi shear** by $C_{AB}=\lim_{r\to\infty}r(\gamma_{AB}-q_{AB})$, the **Bondi news** by $N_{AB}:=\partial_u C_{AB}$, and the **geometric Bondi mass** by $m_B(u):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}m(u,x)\,d\Omega$. The future null boundary used here is the formal $r\to\infty$ boundary $\mathcal I^+=I\times S^2$ with coordinates $(u,x^A)$; no conformal completion is included in this definition. A **vacuum Bondi expansion** means, in addition, that the Ricci tensor $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ defined by the curvature convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] vanishes to the asymptotic coefficient orders under discussion, with no cosmological term.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth Lorentzian bundle conventions of the suppliers. Let a vacuum Bondi expansion be as in [[def-gr-fx-bondi-expansion]], with $R_{ab}=0$ in the curvature convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then, for the mass aspect $m$, shear $C_{AB}$, news $N_{AB}=\partial_uC_{AB}$, unit sphere metric $q_{AB}$ and its Levi-Civita derivative $D_A$ specified there,

$$\partial_um=\frac14D_AD_BN^{AB}-\frac18N_{AB}N^{AB}.$$

The identity is the leading supplementary vacuum Einstein coefficient at future null infinity; it is not an exact finite-radius equation.

Assume Countable Choice and a smooth Bondi expansion as in [[def-gr-fx-bondi-expansion]]. For $u_1<u_2$ in its retarded-length interval, define $\Delta C_{AB}:=C_{AB}(u_2)-C_{AB}(u_1)$. Then

$$\Delta C_{AB}=\int_{u_1}^{u_2}N_{AB}(u)\,du.$$

For the detector clause, fix an angular point $x\in S^2$ and a large fixed area radius $r>r_0$. In the local flat approximation choose the future unit observer $n=\partial_0$ and outward unit propagation direction $\hat k=\partial_3$ of [[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]], so the positive screen is $\Sigma(n,\hat k)=\operatorname{span}(\partial_1,\partial_2)$. Let $\iota:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ be the unit-sphere inclusion; $d\iota_x$ identifies $T_xS^2$ isometrically, for $q$, with the plane orthogonal to $\iota(x)$. Choose axes with $e_3=\iota(x)$ and a fixed ordered orthonormal screen basis $e_1,e_2$ corresponding to a $q$-orthonormal basis of $T_xS^2$. Use adapted inertial coordinates with $x^0=ct$ and $x^3$ in the $\hat k$ direction. The background central worldline is the restriction to $[u_1,u_2]$ of the smooth future-directed timelike affine geodesic $\gamma_0(u)=(x^0=u+r,x^1=0,x^2=0,x^3=r)$; its affine parameter $u$ is also proper-length parameter, and on it the Bondi retarded coordinate is $u=x^0-r$.

A **linear transverse detector approximation** here is the formal flat first-order model with a dimensionless screen-TT profile $H_{AB}(u)=C_{AB}(u,x)/r+\rho_{AB}(u,r,x)$ in the chosen basis, extended on an open tube $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^4$ around $\gamma_0([u_1,u_2])$ as the planar perturbation $h_{AB}(x^0,x^3)=H_{AB}(x^0-x^3)$ with all other components zero. Take $H$ as the first-order coefficient of a smooth flat linearized metric family on $\Omega$; only this coefficient is used. Assume the profile has a smooth extension outside $[u_1,u_2]$; only its values on this interval enter. For $j=0,1,2$, assume $\sup_{u\in[u_1,u_2]}|\partial_u^j\rho_{AB}(u,r,x)|\le K_jr^{-2}$, where the constants $K_j$ are uniform on the fixed interval and angular patch and have dimensions $\mathrm{length}^{2-j}$. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The scalar $Y$ is smooth because it is the restriction of a polynomial on $\mathbb R^3$. By contraction, $q^{AB}T_{AB}=D^2Y-\tfrac12(2)D^2Y=0$. In spherical coordinates at the equator $\theta=\pi/2$, $D_\theta D_\theta Y=3$, $D_\phi D_\phi Y=0$, and $D^2Y=3$, so $T_{\theta\theta}=3/2\ne0$. Thus $T$ is a nonzero smooth trace-free tensor.

For dimensionless $z$, define $b(z)=e^{-1/(1-z^2)}$ for $|z|<1$ and $b(z)=0$ for $|z|\ge1$. Every derivative of the interior formula is a polynomial in $(1-z^2)^{-1}$ and $z$ times $e^{-1/(1-z^2)}$, which tends to zero at both endpoints; hence the zero extension is smooth. With $Z=\int_{-1}^{1}b(z)\,dz>0$, the change of variable $z=u/\tau$ shows that $g_\tau(u)=b(u/\tau)/(\tau Z)$ is smooth, nonnegative, supported on $[-\tau,\tau]$, has units $\mathrm{length}^{-1}$, and has integral one. Its primitive $\Phi_\tau(u)=\int_{-\infty}^u g_\tau(v)\,dv$ is smooth, equals $0$ for $u\le-\tau$, equals $1$ for $u\ge\tau$, and has derivative $g_\tau$.

The fields $C_{AB}=a\Phi_\tau T_{AB}$ and $N_{AB}=ag_\tau T_{AB}$ are smooth and trace-free, and $N=\partial_uC$. Therefore $\Delta C_{AB}=aT_{AB}$ by the normalization $\int g_\tau=1$. Define
$$m(u,x):=\frac14D_AD_B\bigl(C^{AB}(u,x)-C^{AB}(-\tau,x)\bigr)-\frac18\int_{-\tau}^{u}N_{AB}(v,x)N^{AB}(v,x)\,dv.$$
This is smooth, has $m(-\tau,x)=0$, and direct differentiation verifies the imposed local coefficient equation [F2]. The metric construction [L1] gives a smooth Bondi-Sachs end with these coefficients, but does not impose the vacuum Ricci equations.

Let $X^A:=D_BT^{AB}$. In spherical coordinates, $D_AX^A\,d\Omega=\{\partial_\theta(\sin\theta X^\theta)+\partial_\phi(\sin\theta X^\phi)\}\,d\theta\,d\phi$. The $\phi$ boundary terms cancel by periodicity, and smoothness of $X$ makes its meridional component $X^\theta$ bounded near either pole, so $\sin\theta X^\theta\to0$ there. Hence $\int_{S^2}D_AD_BT^{AB}\,d\Omega=0$. Integrating the explicit $m$ from step 2.1 over the sphere therefore yields
$$m_B(\tau)-m_B(-\tau)=-\frac{a^2}{32\pi}\left(\int_{-\tau}^{\tau}g_\tau(u)^2\,du\right)\left(\int_{S^2}T_{AB}T^{AB}\,d\Omega\right).$$
The time integral is positive because $g_\tau$ is continuous and has unit integral. The sphere integral is positive because $q$ is positive definite and $T$ is continuous and nonzero by step 1.1. Since $a\ne0$, the mass change is strictly negative. This derivation uses only the imposed coefficient equation, not the smooth-vacuum mass-loss proposition.

The pulse has $N(-\tau)=N(\tau)=0$, so [F3] applies. Its integrated shear change is $\Delta C=aT$, hence the formal first-order detector response is $\delta s^A(\tau)=\tfrac{a}{2r}T^A{}_Bs_0^B+O(r^{-2}|s_0|)$. The finite-radius qualification is the stated one; the formal calculation uses no nonlinear amplitude remainder.

If the normalized local family in the Example is supplied, apply the quantitative clause of [F3] with $u_1=-\tau$, $u_2=\tau$ and $\Delta C=aT$. The news vanishes at both endpoints because the smooth bump and all its derivatives vanish there. The result is the displayed actual Jacobi displacement and velocity estimate, with exactly that theorem's fixed-family amplitude constants. This uses the imposed formal boundary coefficients and detector-family hypotheses, not an inference of a vacuum metric or a measurement.

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

derivations.claim:
The set $[0,2\pi]\times[t_n-k,t_n+k]$ is a nonempty closed box in
$\mathbb R^2$: $k>0$ and the time interval lies in $I$. Thus [F4] makes it
compact. The function $(x,t)\mapsto u_{xxxx}(x,t)$ is continuous there because
$u\in C^6$; [F5] bounds it, so $M_n<\infty$ as claimed.

Apply [F2] to the spatial function $x\mapsto u(x,t_n)$ at $x_j$ with
increments $h$ and $-h$. Adding the two degree-three Taylor polynomials and
subtracting twice their common center value cancels their odd terms and leaves $h^2u_{xx}(x_j,t_n)$. By [F2], each remainder has absolute value at
most $M_nh^4/4!$; by [F7], the sum of the two remainders has absolute value
at most $2M_nh^4/4!$. After division by $h^2$,
$$
\left|\frac{U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n}{h^2}-u_{xx}(x_j,t_n)\right| \le\frac{h^2}{12}M_n.
$$
Periodicity of $u$ and its derivatives extends the bound defining $M_n$ from
$[0,2\pi]$ to all real spatial coordinates, including a wrapped neighbor.

Apply the same estimate to $t\mapsto u(x_j,t)$ with increments $k$ and
$-k$. By [F3] and $u_{tt}=u_{xx}$, the fourth time derivative equals
$u_{tttt}=u_{xxxx}$, whose absolute value is bounded by $M_n$ on this time
window and all $x$. Thus
$$
\left|\frac{U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}}{k^2}-u_{tt}(x_j,t_n)\right| \le\frac{k^2}{12}M_n.
$$

Subtract the two estimates of steps 1.2 and 1.3, use
$u_{tt}(x_j,t_n)=u_{xx}(x_j,t_n)$, and apply the real triangle inequality
[F7] to their error terms. The result is
$|\tau_j^n|\le(k^2+h^2)M_n/12$, as claimed.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: From the Clifford relation, $\gamma^I\gamma^J\gamma^K=2\eta^{JK}\gamma^I-2\eta^{IK}\gamma^J+\gamma^K\gamma^I\gamma^J$. Subtracting $\gamma^K\gamma^I\gamma^J$ gives $[\gamma^I\gamma^J,\gamma^K]=2(\eta^{JK}\gamma^I-\eta^{IK}\gamma^J)$. This is an algebraic identity for every triple of indices, including repeated indices, and uses no group-representation covariance hypothesis.

Contract step 1.1 with $\frac14\omega_{IJ}$. Since $\omega_{IJ}\eta^{JK}=-\omega^K{}_I$ by antisymmetry and $\omega_{IJ}\eta^{IK}=\omega^K{}_J$, the two terms each contribute $-\frac12\omega^K{}_J\gamma^J$ after relabeling the summed index. Hence $[\Gamma,\gamma^K]=-\omega^K{}_J\gamma^J$. The contraction is valid because each $\omega_{IJ}$ is scalar-valued and the gamma matrices are constant in the chosen local frame.

Write $c(V)=V_K\gamma^K$. Then step 2.1 gives $dc(V)+[\Gamma,c(V)]=dV_K\gamma^K-V_K\omega^K{}_J\gamma^J=(dV_J-\omega^K{}_J V_K)\gamma^J=c(
abla V)$. For a spinor $\psi$, expand $D(c(V)\psi)=d(c(V)\psi)+\Gamma c(V)\psi$ and use
$\Gamma c(V)=c(V)\Gamma+[\Gamma,c(V)]$. The result is
$c(
abla V)\psi+c(V)(d\psi+\Gamma\psi)=c(
abla V)\psi+c(V)D\psi$, as asserted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $u^*$ denote the continuous absolutely
continuous representative of a class in $H^1$ supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]], and write
$\|u\|=\|u\|_{L^2}$ and $\|u'\|=\|u'\|_{L^2}$ for the norms of
[[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]] on the interval under
consideration.

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.
Then $T$ is closable if and only if $D(T^*)$ is dense in $H$. In that case
$\overline T=T^{**}$ and $T^*=\overline T^{\,*}$; moreover if $T\subseteq T^*$,
then $T$ is closable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Density follows from [F3]. For $f,g\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$, integration by
parts gives $\langle -f'',g\rangle=\langle f,-g''\rangle$, since both
functions and their derivatives vanish near the endpoints. Thus $T_c$ is
dense and symmetric.

Suppose $u\in L^2(0,L)$ has distributional second derivative
$D^2u=h\in L^2(0,L)$. By [F6], $h\in L^1(0,L)$. Define
$v(x)=\int_0^x h(t)\,dt$. Then $|v(x)|\le\|h\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt L\|h\|_2$,
so $v\in L^2(0,L)$. For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$, choose a
measurable representative of $h$ and define
$$G(t,x):=\mathbf 1_{\{0<t<x<L\}}h(t)\varphi'(x),\qquad (t,x)\in(0,L)^2.$$
The function $q(t,x)=|h(t)||\varphi'(x)|$ is nonnegative and
product-measurable. By [F6], $h\in L^1(0,L)$. The test derivative
$\varphi'$ is continuous with compact support in $(0,L)$, hence belongs to
$L^2(0,L)$; [F6] then gives $\varphi'\in L^1(0,L)$. Tonelli [F8], applied only to
this nonnegative product, gives
$$\int_{(0,L)^2}q\,d(\lambda\times\lambda)=\left(\int_0^L|h(t)|\,dt\right)\left(\int_0^L|\varphi'(x)|\,dx\right)<\infty.$$
Since $|G|\le q$, this establishes $G\in L^1((0,L)^2)$ without using
Fubini to prove its own hypothesis. Its sections are integrable for every
parameter because $h,\varphi'\in L^1(0,L)$. Fubini [F9] therefore gives
$$\int_0^L v(x)\varphi'(x)\,dx=\int_0^L\int_0^x h(t)\varphi'(x)\,dt\,dx=\int_0^Lh(t)\left(\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx\right)dt=-\int_0^Lh(t)\varphi(t)\,dt,$$
where [F7] applied to real and imaginary parts gives
$\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx=\varphi(L)-\varphi(t)=-\varphi(t)$, since
$\varphi$ vanishes near $L$. Hence $Dv=h$ weakly and $v\in H^1$.
The distribution $Du-v$ has derivative zero. For every test function
$\varphi$ of integral zero, its primitive
$\psi(x)=\int_0^x\varphi(t)\,dt$ is compactly supported in $(0,L)$, and hence
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(D\psi)=-(D(Du-v))(\psi)=0$. Obtain a test
function $\eta$ with integral one as follows. The constant function $1$ lies
in $L^2(0,L)$ with norm $\sqrt L$. By the density in [F3], choose
$\chi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ with $\|\chi-1\|_2<\sqrt L/2$; then
$\|\chi\|_2>\sqrt L/2$. Set $\eta=|\chi|^2/\|\chi\|_2^2$. It is a smooth
compactly supported test function and $\int_0^L\eta=1$. For arbitrary
$\varphi$,
$\varphi-(\int_0^L\varphi)\eta$ has integral zero, so
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(\eta)\int_0^L\varphi$. Therefore $Du-v$ is a constant
distribution, $Du=v+c\in L^2$, and $u\in H^2(0,L)$ by [F1].

If $g\in H^2(0,L)$, [F2] applied with a compactly supported test function
shows $\langle T_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,-D^2g\rangle$; thus
$g\in D(T_c^*)$ and $T_c^*g=-D^2g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(T_c^*)$ and
$h=T_c^*g$, testing the adjoint identity against every
$f\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2g=-h\in L^2$. Step 1.2
then gives $g\in H^2(0,L)$. Hence $T_c^*=T_{\max}$ with exactly the claimed
domain.

By [F5] and step 2.1, $T_{\min}=T_c^{**}=T_{\max}^*$. If
$u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$ and $h=T_{\max}^*u$, testing against
$C_c^\infty(0,L)\subset H^2(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2u=-h$.
Step 1.2 implies $u\in H^2(0,L)$. The adjoint identity for all
$g\in H^2(0,L)$ and [F2] now reads
$\langle\Gamma_1g,\Gamma_0u\rangle-\langle\Gamma_0g,\Gamma_1u\rangle=0$.
By step 1.3 the two traces of $g$ can be prescribed independently: first set
$\Gamma_0g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_1g$ to obtain $\Gamma_0u=0$; then set
$\Gamma_1g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_0g$ to obtain $\Gamma_1u=0$. Conversely, if
$u\in H^2$ has both traces zero, [F2] gives
$\langle T_{\max}g,u\rangle=\langle g,-D^2u\rangle$ for every
$g\in H^2$, so $u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$. Therefore
$D(T_{\min})=\{u\in H^2:\Gamma_0u=\Gamma_1u=0\}$ and its action is
$-D^2u$.

The preceding steps establish density, symmetry, the exact adjoint, the
closure domain, and trace surjectivity as stated.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open energy interval with fixed finite channel number $r\ge1$, let $S:I\to U(r)$ be $C^1$ in the finite-channel convention of [[def-nrqmx-scattering-channel-data]], and let $\hbar>0$. Define

$$Q(E):=-i\hbar\,S(E)^*S'(E),\qquad E\in I.$$

Then $Q(E)$ is Hermitian and

$$\operatorname{tr}Q(E) =-i\hbar\,\frac{(\det S)'(E)}{\det S(E)} =-i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dE}\log\det S(E),$$

where the last expression means the logarithmic derivative $(\det S)'/\det S$, independent of a choice of logarithm branch. If the incoming and outgoing bases are changed by energy-independent unitary matrices $U_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $U_{\mathrm{out}}$, so that $S^\sharp=U_{\mathrm{out}}^*SU_{\mathrm{in}}$, then

$$Q^\sharp=U_{\mathrm{in}}^* Q U_{\mathrm{in}}.$$

If $E$ is measured in joules and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, $Q$ has units of seconds. This is an algebraic scattering-matrix result; it does not by itself establish an operational arrival-time or dwell-time interpretation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $0<\epsilon\leq1$, and set $N_d=4d+4$. For a smooth $a:\mathbb R^{2d}\to\mathbb C$ with $\partial^\alpha a$ bounded for every $|\alpha|\leq N_d$, define

$$ \mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}\,dy $$

for $u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, and define the Weyl operator initially as the form

$$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi . $$

There is a unique bounded operator $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ representing this form, and

$$ \|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq C_d\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty , $$

where $C_d$ depends only on $d$. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, this extension agrees with the kernel definition in [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner].

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
Since $a$ is compactly supported and smooth, Fourier inversion in its $\xi$ variable identifies $K_{\epsilon,a}((x+y)/2,x-y)$ with the kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$. Its derivatives have rapid decay in $x-y$, uniformly on compact sets of $(x+y)/2$, by [F3]. To justify the potential term on Schwartz vectors, fix $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and put $g(s)=V(sx)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F6] applied twice and Fubini [F4], $$ V(x)=V(0)+
abla V(0)\cdot x+\int_0^1(1-s)\,x^T D^2V(sx)x\,ds. $$ Thus boundedness of $D^2V$ gives $|V(x)|\le C(1+|x|^2)$. Applying [F6] once to each component of $
abla V(sx)$ also gives $|
abla V(x)|\le C(1+|x|)$, while all derivatives of $V$ of order at least $2$ are bounded by hypothesis. Hence every derivative of $V$ has at most polynomial growth. The product rule [F5] and Schwartz seminorm bounds show $Vu\in\mathcal S$ whenever $u\in\mathcal S$; differentiation also preserves $\mathcal S$. Therefore $H_\epsilon^0$ and the commutator in the Statement are well defined on $\mathcal S$.

Write $q=(x+y)/2$ and $r=x-y$. Then $\partial_x=\frac12\partial_q+\partial_r$, $\partial_y=\frac12\partial_q-\partial_r$, so $\partial_x^2-\partial_y^2=2\partial_q\cdot\partial_r$. Acting with the kinetic operator on the two kernel variables gives $[-\epsilon^2\Delta/2,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)]$ kernel $-\epsilon^2\partial_q\cdot\partial_rK_{\epsilon,a}$. Since $\partial_{r_j}e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}=i\xi_j e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}/\epsilon$, multiplication by $i/\epsilon$ turns this exactly into the Weyl kernel with symbol $\xi\cdot\nabla_xa$.

The potential part has kernel $(V(q+r/2)-V(q-r/2))K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$. To derive its Taylor remainder, fix $q,r$ and set $g(s)=V(q+sr)$ for $s\in[-1/2,1/2]$. Applying [F6] three times to $g$ and to $s\mapsto g(-s)$, with Fubini [F4] to combine the resulting integrals, gives for $0\le t\le1/2$ $$ g(t)=g(0)+tg'(0)+ rac{t^2}{2}g''(0)+ rac12\int_0^t(t-s)^2g'''(s)\,ds, $$ $$ g(-t)=g(0)-tg'(0)+ rac{t^2}{2}g''(0)- rac12\int_0^t(t-s)^2g'''(-s)\,ds. $$ Subtract at $t=1/2$ and substitute $s=	au/2$ in the two remainder integrals. Since $g'''(s)=D^3V(q+sr)[r,r,r]$, this yields $$ V(q+r/2)-V(q-r/2)=r\cdot
abla V(q)+\Delta_V(q,r), $$ $$ \Delta_V(q,r)= rac1{16}\int_0^1(1-s)^2\left(D^3V(q+sr/2)[r,r,r]+D^3V(q-sr/2)[r,r,r]ight)\,ds . $$ Integration by parts in $\xi$ is justified coordinatewise by [F7] and Fubini [F4]: the factors $e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)$ are compactly supported in $\xi$, their derivative products are integrable, and their endpoint products vanish. It gives $\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}r_j a(q,\xi)\,d\xi=i\epsilon\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}\partial_{\xi_j}a(q,\xi)\,d\xi$. Therefore the linear term, multiplied by $i/\epsilon$, is the Weyl kernel with symbol $-
abla_\xi a\cdot
abla V$. Together with step 2.1 this is exactly $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{a,h\})$.

The kernel $K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$ is compactly supported in $q$ and Schwartz in $r$, since $a\in C_c^\infty$. The formula derived in step 3.1, applied also to each $\partial_q^\alpha V$, and the bounded derivatives of $V$ show that $\Delta_V(q,r)$ and all its $q,r$ derivatives grow at most polynomially in $r$, uniformly for $q$ in that compact set. Hence $G(q,r):=\Delta_V(q,r)K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$ is Schwartz in $(q,r)$; its partial Fourier transform is Schwartz by [F3], and Fourier inversion [F3] recovers $G$. Define the remainder symbol by the inverse partial Fourier transform $$ r_{\epsilon,a,V}(q,\eta):=\frac{i}{\epsilon^3}\int e^{-ir\cdot\eta/\epsilon}\Delta_V(q,r)K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)\,dr. $$ By construction its Weyl kernel is $i\epsilon^{-3}\Delta_V(q,r)K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$, so the remaining potential commutator kernel, after multiplication by $i/\epsilon$, is $\epsilon^2$ times that kernel. Apply [F8] to the positive scaling $s\mapsto r=\epsilon s$ in this absolutely integrable complex Fourier integral. This gives $$ r_{\epsilon,a,V}(q,\eta)=i(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{-is\cdot\eta}\frac{\Delta_V(q,\epsilon s)}{\epsilon^3}\left(\int e^{is\cdot\xi}a(q,\xi)\,d\xi\right)ds. $$ For $|\alpha|\le N_d$, the formula from step 3.1 applied to $\partial_q^\alpha V$ gives $|\partial_q^\alpha\Delta_V(q,\epsilon s)|\le C_{\alpha,V}\epsilon^3|s|^3$, since every third derivative of $\partial_q^\alpha V$ is bounded by hypothesis. Derivatives in $\eta$ insert powers of $s$; derivatives in $q$ of the partial Fourier transform insert derivatives of $a$. Repeated coordinatewise integration by parts in $\xi$, justified by [F7], gives decay factor $(1+|s|^2)^{-4d-5}$ uniformly in $q$, with zero boundary terms because $a$ is compactly supported in $\xi$. For $|\alpha|\le N_d$, the largest remaining radial power is $|s|^{N_d+3}=|s|^{4d+7}$; after the $d$-dimensional radial measure, the tail is bounded by a constant times $\int_1^\infty\rho^{-3d-4}d\rho<\infty$. More explicitly, bounding all $q,\eta$ derivatives of total order at most $N_d$ uses $(1-\Delta_\xi)^{4d+5}$ on $a$, hence at most $N_d+8d+10=12d+14$ derivatives, within $M_d=12d+16$. This proves the stated uniform derivative bound.

Apply [F2] to $r_{\epsilon,a,V}$. Its bounded derivatives through $N_d$, established in step 4.1, imply $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a,V})\|\leq C_{d,V}p_{M_d}(a)$, uniformly for $0<\epsilon\leq1$. Combining steps 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 proves the commutator identity on $\mathcal S$ and the asserted operator-norm bound on its remainder.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $0<\epsilon\leq1$, and set $N_d=4d+4$. For a smooth $a:\mathbb R^{2d}\to\mathbb C$ with $\partial^\alpha a$ bounded for every $|\alpha|\leq N_d$, define

$$ \mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}\,dy $$

for $u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, and define the Weyl operator initially as the form

$$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi . $$

There is a unique bounded operator $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ representing this form, and

$$ \|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq C_d\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty , $$

where $C_d$ depends only on $d$. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, this extension agrees with the kernel definition in [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
