citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A boundary chart is a homeomorphism $\varphi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb H^n$, where $U\subseteq M$ is open and $V$ is relatively open. Two charts are compatible if each transition map is smooth in the local-extension sense. A smooth atlas is a compatible covering atlas; its smooth structure is its maximal compatible atlas.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

For an oriented manifold with boundary, orient $T_p\partial M$ by the **outward-normal-first** rule: an outward vector first, followed by a positive boundary determinant, is a positive determinant of $T_pM$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

derivations.claim: By compactness and [F2], choose finitely many $C^2$ straightening neighborhoods of $D$ with compact coordinate closures, using the local models in the Statement at points on $\partial M$. At an interior boundary arc with parametrization $\gamma(s)$, choose a transverse vector $v$ and use $(s,t)\mapsto\gamma(s)+tv$; its derivative is invertible, so [F8] gives a $C^2$ inverse chart. At a corner in an interior chart, the independent tangent vectors of the two incident arcs make $(s,t)\mapsto\gamma_1(s)+\gamma_2(t)-\gamma_1(0)$ a $C^2$ local diffeomorphism by [F8]; it straightens the boundary to coordinate axes and the region to a quadrant or its reentrant complement. Add $M\setminus D$ to this finite open cover and use [F3] for a smooth subordinate partition of unity. On $D$, only finitely many localized forms $\eta_i=\rho_i\eta$ contribute, each with compact support in one straightening chart.

In an oriented coordinate plane, a compactly supported $C^1$ form $a\,dx+b\,dy$ satisfies $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)=0$, $\int_{y\geq0}(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)=\int_{\mathbb R}a(x,0)\,dx$, and $\int_{x,y\geq0}(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)=\int_0^\infty a(x,0)\,dx-\int_0^\infty b(0,y)\,dy$. For complex coefficients, apply the calculation to real and imaginary parts. Put the support in a rectangle; [F9] makes the coefficients and their first derivatives Riemann integrable, and [F10] makes them uniformly continuous. Double Riemann sums and iterated one-dimensional Riemann sums have the same limit, since their difference is bounded by the rectangle area times the modulus of continuity at the mesh diameter. Then [F7] evaluates the one-dimensional integrals of $\partial_xb$ and $\partial_ya$ at their endpoints, and the compact support removes the artificial outer edges. The half-plane and quadrant boundary signs are exactly the outward-normal-first convention [F6]. On the reentrant model, subtract the missing open quadrant from the plane; the two axis integrals have the opposite orientation, so the same identity holds.

A $C^2$ straightening map preserves the exterior derivative of a $C^1$ one-form by the chain rule: the terms involving its second derivatives cancel by symmetry. The compact-support change-of-variables formula [F4] carries each local area identity to $D$, while [F6] carries the axis orientations to the oriented boundary arcs. Summing over the partition from step 1.1 gives $\int_Dd\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta$. The empty region and empty boundary give zero on both sides.

Let $q_0:=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}\in C_2(\mathbb R^2)$. There is a pointed
homeomorphism
$$\bigl(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0\bigr)\cong \bigl(\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, (0,1,[0])\bigr),$$
and
$$\pi_1(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0)\cong(\mathbb Z,+).$$
Under the isomorphism specified in the proof, the counterclockwise exchange
loop
$$\gamma(t):=\{(\cos\pi t,\sin\pi t),(-\cos\pi t,-\sin\pi t)\},\qquad 0\leq t\leq1,$$
is a positive generator. The loop in which the relative direction makes one
full counterclockwise turn is $[\gamma]^2$, so it represents twice the
generator.

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.

A **universal covering space** of $B$ is a covering map $p:\widetilde B\to B$ whose total space $\widetilde B$ is simply connected ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]], [[def-simply-connected]]).

For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ ([[def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces]]). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation ([[def-group]], [[def-group-action]]).

Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Use the pointed coordinate identification
$$C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,$$
which sends $q_0=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}$ to $(0,1,[0])$, to write
$$X:=C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z.$$
Put $\widetilde X:=\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ and define
$$p(c,\rho,t):=(c,\rho,[t])\in X,\qquad T_n(c,\rho,t):=(c,\rho,t+n)\quad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$
Define $U(1):=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ under complex multiplication. Let
$\chi:\mathbb Z\to U(1)$ satisfy
$\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(m+n)=\chi(m)\chi(n)$ for all $m,n\in\mathbb Z$.
Let $\mathbb Z$ act on
$\widetilde X\times\mathbb C$ by
$$n\cdot((c,\rho,t),z):=((c,\rho,t+n),\chi(n)^{-1}z).$$
The homomorphism law for $\chi$ makes this a group action, and its orbits
define the quotient relation.
Define the **character quotient** and its projection by
$$L_\chi:=(\widetilde X\times\mathbb C)/\mathbb Z, \qquad \Pi_\chi([\widetilde x,z]):=p(\widetilde x),$$
with the quotient topology on $L_\chi$. Since $p(T_n\widetilde x)=p(\widetilde x)$,
it induces a continuous map $\Pi_\chi:L_\chi\to X$. Once $p$ is known to be
a covering map, the **monodromy** of this quotient around a based loop means
the fiber map obtained by lifting the loop and keeping its complex coordinate
$z$ constant along the lift.

For this item, a **unitary flat complex line bundle** over a space $X$ means a
continuous surjection $\Pi:L\to X$ with local trivializations
$\Pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb C$ over open sets $U$, whose changes of fiber
coordinate on overlaps are multiplication by functions $g:U\cap V\to U(1)$
that are locally constant (constant on some neighbourhood of each point).
The definition above names the quotient data; the following theorem verifies
that $L_\chi$ has these line-bundle and flatness properties.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.

derivations.claim:
The projection $p(c,\rho,t)=(c,\rho,[t])$ is continuous and surjective.
For any $[t_0]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, choose an open interval
$I=(a,b)$ around a representative of $[t_0]$ with $b-a<1$. Its image is an
open arc because its full preimage $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}(I+n)$ is open
by [F5, F7]; the translates are disjoint by $b-a<1$. On each sheet $I+n$,
the quotient map $t\mapsto[t]$ is a homeomorphism onto that arc: it is a
continuous bijection and maps open subsets to open subsets by the same
saturation check. Taking products with the other two coordinate factors
gives evenly covered open neighborhoods in $X$, so [F2] makes $p$ a covering
map.

By [F4], a deck transformation $D$ satisfies $pD=p$. Hence $D$ fixes
the $\mathbb R^2$ and $(0,\infty)$ coordinates and has last coordinate
$t+k(c,\rho,t)$ for an integer-valued continuous function $k$, by [F5].
The space $\widetilde X$ is connected because it is convex: its radius
coordinate stays positive on every line segment. Therefore $k$ is constant;
thus $D=T_n$ for some
$n\in\mathbb Z$. Conversely each $T_n$ preserves $p$ and is a homeomorphism,
so these are exactly the deck transformations.

The space $\widetilde X$ is nonempty and convex in $\mathbb R^4$ because
the radius coordinate remains positive along every line segment. For any
basepoint $x_0\in\widetilde X$ and based loop $\alpha$, the straight-line
homotopy $H_s(t)=(1-s)\alpha(t)+s x_0$ remains in $\widetilde X$ and fixes
both endpoints. Thus every based loop from [F9] is null-homotopic, so [F6]
makes $\widetilde X$ simply connected. By [F3], $p$ is a universal covering
map.

The action in [F8] is a group action: composing the $m$ and $n$ actions
adds the shifts and multiplies the fiber coordinate by
$\chi(m)^{-1}\chi(n)^{-1}=\chi(m+n)^{-1}$. The action is free because
$T_n\widetilde x=\widetilde x$ implies $n=0$. If $U$ is an evenly covered
neighborhood as in step 1.1 and $V$ is one chosen sheet, every orbit over
$U$ has exactly one representative in $V\times\mathbb C$. The quotient
topology therefore identifies $\Pi_\chi^{-1}(U)$ homeomorphically with
$U\times\mathbb C$: the restriction from $V\times\mathbb C$ is bijective,
and it is open because the saturation of an open subset is the union of its
translates under the homeomorphisms in [F8]. The fiber coordinate is the
unique representative's complex coordinate. This gives a local trivialization
with one-dimensional complex fibers.

On an overlap, two chosen sheets differ locally by a fixed translation
$T_n$, because the sheets of a covering are disjoint and indexed by the
discrete integers. The corresponding fiber coordinate changes by
$z\mapsto\chi(n)z$ or its inverse, according to the direction of the chart
change. Since $|\chi(n)|=1$ and $n$ is locally constant, these transition
functions are locally constant $U(1)$-valued functions. By [F8], this is a
unitary flat complex line bundle.

Let a based loop have a lift from $\widetilde x$ to $T_n\widetilde x$;
the path-lifting theorem [F10] supplies a unique lift from every prescribed
starting point. Keeping $z$ constant along this lift gives endpoint class
$[T_n\widetilde x,z]$. The defining equivalence in [F8] gives
$[T_n\widetilde x,z]=[\widetilde x,\chi(n)z]$, so monodromy is multiplication
by $\chi(n)$. The explicit positive exchange path has lifted angle coordinate
$t\mapsto t$ from $0$ to $1$, while the full relative turn has $t\mapsto2t$
from $0$ to $2$, by the homeomorphism in [F1]. Thus their monodromies are
$\chi(1)$ and $\chi(2)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, fix a positive real action-scale parameter
$\hbar>0$, and let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad
P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$

(a) *Contraction map.* For every $f\in H$ and $n\ge0$ there is a unique bounded
linear map $\Psi_f^{(n)}:H^{\otimes(n+1)}\to H^{\otimes n}$ with
$$\langle\varphi,\Psi_f^{(n)}\chi\rangle=\langle f\otimes\varphi,\chi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in H^{\otimes n},\ \chi\in H^{\otimes(n+1)})$$
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); it satisfies
$\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\|\le\|f\|$,
$\Psi_f^{(n)}(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1})=\langle u_1,f\rangle\,u_2\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1}$
on elementary tensors, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$,
and the map $f\mapsto\Psi_f^{(n)}$ is conjugate-linear.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
Apply [F4] to the diffeomorphism $x\mapsto e^{-s}x$ and
$|f|^2\in L^1$:
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|e^{-s/2}f(e^{-s}x)|^2dx =\int_{\mathbb R}|f(y)|^2dy,$$
and $U_s$ is unitary. For Schwartz $f$, direct substitution and the chain rule give
$$U_s^*QU_sf=e^sQf,\qquad U_s^*PU_sf=e^{-s}Pf.$$
Using $a=(Q+iP)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ and
$a^*=(Q-iP)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$, this becomes
$$U_s^*aU_s=\frac{e^s+e^{-s}}2a+ \frac{e^s-e^{-s}}2a^*=\cosh(s)a+\sinh(s)a^*.$$
The dilation maps Schwartz space onto itself, so all identities hold on the
stated common core and the associated Weyl covariance extends everywhere by
unitarity.

The ground function $g_0(x)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$ is even, so its
position mean is zero; its derivative is odd, so its momentum mean is zero.
By [F3] with $A=1,B=0$, $\int e^{-x^2}dx=\sqrt\pi$. On $[-R,R]$,
the finite-interval integration-by-parts supplier in [F3] gives
$$\int_{-R}^R x^2e^{-x^2}dx=\left[-\frac{x}{2}e^{-x^2}\right]_{-R}^R+\frac12\int_{-R}^Re^{-x^2}dx.$$
The boundary term tends to zero by [F3], so
$\int x^2|g_0(x)|^2dx=\pi^{-1/2}(\sqrt\pi/2)=1/2$. Also
$g_0'=-xg_0$ gives both vacuum variances $\hbar/2$. Moreover
$\langle Q\Omega,P\Omega\rangle=-i\hbar/2$, so the real symmetrized cross
covariance is zero. For $\psi_s=U_s\Omega$, the unitary conjugation formulas
in step 1.1 give
$$\langle Q\rangle_{\psi_s}=e^s\langle Q\rangle_\Omega=0, \quad \langle Q^2\rangle_{\psi_s}=e^{2s}\hbar/2,$$
and likewise $\langle P\rangle_{\psi_s}=0$ and
$\langle P^2\rangle_{\psi_s}=e^{-2s}\hbar/2$. The cross form is unchanged
because the two scale factors multiply to one, so it remains zero. Therefore
the covariance determinant is the product of the two variances,
$\hbar^2/4$.

Since $U_s$ maps Schwartz space to itself, $\psi_s$ is in the domain of
the number form. By [F2] and step 2.1,
$$\langle a^*a\rangle_{\psi_s} =\frac{\langle Q^2+P^2\rangle_{\psi_s}}{2\hbar}-\frac12 =\frac{e^{2s}+e^{-2s}-2}{4}=\sinh^2(s).$$
This is the model's finite one-mode number expectation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let
$S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ with angular coordinate $\phi$, and identify
$L^2(S^1;\mathbb C)$ with $L^2((0,2\pi),d\phi;\mathbb C)$; the omitted
endpoint has measure zero. Let $H^2(0,2\pi)$ be the interval Sobolev space whose elements and first two weak derivatives are in $L^2$. For $f\in H^2(0,2\pi)$ use the continuous endpoint representatives of $f$ and $f'$, and denote their traces by $f^*(0),f^*(2\pi)$ and $(f')^*(0),(f')^*(2\pi)$. Define
the periodic second-order domain
$$H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)=\{f\in H^2(0,2\pi):f^*(0)=f^*(2\pi),\ (f')^*(0)=(f')^*(2\pi)\}.$$
It is the domain used for the periodic realization of the second derivative;
it imposes no boundary at the angular seam beyond periodic matching.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$0<L<\infty$, let $H=L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, and let $T_{\min}$ and
$T_{\max}=T_{\min}^*$ be the minimal and maximal realizations of
$-D^2$ from the preceding interval-domain lemma. Fix a positive reference
length $\ell$. For $f\in H^2(0,L)$ define
$\Gamma_0f=(f(0),f(L))$ and
$\Gamma_1f=(f'(0),-f'(L))$. Let
$U(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_2\}$, where $U^*$ is conjugate
transpose. For each $U\in U(2)$ define
$$D(T_U)=\{f\in H^2(0,L):(U-I_2)\Gamma_0f+i\ell(U+I_2)\Gamma_1f=0\},\qquad T_Uf=-D^2f.$$
Then $T_{\min}\subseteq T_U\subseteq T_{\max}$, each $T_U$ is self-adjoint,
and every self-adjoint realization between $T_{\min}$ and $T_{\max}$ equals
exactly one $T_U$. The reference length makes the value and scaled derivative
boundary vectors have the same units if the interval coordinate is assigned
units; in the dimensionless mathematical model they are numerical vectors.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axioms of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).
Use the spaces of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]] and the
absolutely continuous representatives supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]].

(a) *Bounded intervals.* Let $0<L<\infty$ and $u,v\in H^1(0,L)$. Then
$\int_0^Lu\,\overline{v'}=u^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}
-\int_0^Lu'\,\overline v .$

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

(c) *Second-order identity.* For $u,v\in H^2(0,L)$,
$\int_0^L\bigl(u''\overline v-u\,\overline{v''}\bigr)
=\bigl[u'^*\overline{v^*}-u^*\overline{v'^*}\bigr]_0^L,$
where the bracket denotes
$u'^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(L)\overline{v'^*(L)}
-u'^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}+u^*(0)\overline{v'^*(0)}$.

(d) *Half-line and line.* If $u,v\in H^1(0,\infty)$, then
$\int_0^\infty u\overline{v'}=-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}-\int_0^\infty u'\overline v$, both integrals
being absolutely convergent. For $u,v\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ one instead has
$\int_{\mathbb R}u\overline{v'}=-\int_{\mathbb R}u'\overline v$,
with both integrals absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim:
Set $A_0=-\kappa\partial_\phi^2$ on $H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$. In the
boundary coordinates $\Gamma_0f=(f(0),f(2\pi))$ and
$\Gamma_1f=(f'(0),-f'(2\pi))$, the unitary swap matrix in [F1] makes the
boundary equation equivalent to $f(0)=f(2\pi)$ and
$f'(0)=f'(2\pi)$: adding and subtracting its two scalar equations gives
these two equalities. Hence $-\partial_\phi^2$ is self-adjoint on this
domain, and multiplication by the positive real $\kappa$ shows that $A_0$
is self-adjoint. Let $P=-i\partial_\phi$.
Integration by parts [F5] and equality of the endpoint traces show that $P$ is
symmetric on $H^2_{\mathrm{per}}$. For $f=\sum_nc_ne_n$ in this domain,
integration by parts gives $\langle Pf,e_n\rangle=nc_n$ and
$\langle A_0f,e_n\rangle=\kappa n^2c_n$. Parseval for [F2] therefore
implies $\|Pf\|_2^2=\sum_n n^2|c_n|^2$ and
$\|A_0f\|_2^2=\kappa^2\sum_n n^4|c_n|^2$.

On $D(A_0)$ write
$T_\alpha=A_0+B_\alpha$ with
$B_\alpha=-2\kappa\alpha P+\kappa\alpha^2I$. This operator is symmetric
because $P$ is symmetric and $\alpha,\kappa$ are real. For every
$\varepsilon>0$ and integer $n$,
$|n|\le\varepsilon n^2+(4\varepsilon)^{-1}$; the coefficient identities
in step 1.1 and the triangle inequality give
$\|B_\alpha f\|_2\le a\|A_0f\|_2+b\|f\|_2$ with any prescribed $a>0$
after choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small and then a finite $b$.
Applying [F3] with $a<1$ proves that $T_\alpha$ is self-adjoint on the
stated periodic domain.

Each $e_n$ lies in the periodic domain and direct differentiation gives
$T_\alpha e_n=\kappa(n-\alpha)^2e_n$. Completeness [F2] makes this the full
orthonormal eigenbasis. The associated spectral projections are therefore
the sums of the character projections whose eigenvalues lie in the chosen
Borel set, so every scalar spectral measure is supported on
$\{\kappa(n-\alpha)^2:n\in\mathbb Z\}$. This set has no finite accumulation
point because $\kappa>0$ and $|n-\alpha|\to\infty$. If $z$ is outside it,
$\inf_n|\lambda_n-z|>0$. For $f=\sum_nc_ne_n$, where
$c_n=\langle f,e_n\rangle$, the diagonal map
$R_zf=\sum_n c_n(\lambda_n-z)^{-1}e_n$ is bounded on $H$. Also
$\sup_n|\lambda_n/(\lambda_n-z)|<\infty$, so the domain characterization
in [F4] shows that $R_z$ maps into $D(T_\alpha)$. Coefficientwise,
$(T_\alpha-z)R_z=I$ and $R_z(T_\alpha-z)=I$ on $D(T_\alpha)$, so $z$ is
in the resolvent. If $z=\lambda_n$ then $e_n$ is a nonzero kernel vector.
Hence the spectrum is exactly the
displayed set and there is no continuous spectral measure.

Let $j\in\mathbb Z$ and $U_jf=e^{ij\phi}f$. It is unitary, preserves
the periodic $H^2$ domain, and
$(P-\alpha-j)U_jf=U_j(P-\alpha)f$ by differentiation; squaring gives
$T_{\alpha+j}U_j=U_jT_\alpha$. If a smooth periodic unit-modulus function
$u$ satisfies the displayed conjugacy, then $(P-\alpha)u=0$, or
$u'=i\alpha u$.
The solutions are $u(\phi)=c e^{i\alpha\phi}$ with $|c|=1$, which are
periodic exactly when $e^{2\pi i\alpha}=1$, equivalently $\alpha\in\mathbb Z$.
Conversely, for integral $\alpha$ this multiplier is single-valued and
periodic.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $r\ge1$, and let $P:M\to M_r(\mathbb C)$ be a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of constant rank $m$, with $1\le m\le r$. Its image bundle is $E_P=\{(x,v):P(x)v=v\}$, with the projected connection $\nabla s=P\,ds$ of [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]]. The **determinant line bundle** is the complex line bundle

For the projector of [[def-nrqmx-determinant-line-projector]], $Q(x)=\bigwedge^mP(x)$ is a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of rank one. Its range is exactly $\det E_P(x)=\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P(x)$, so these ranges form the determinant line bundle.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $r\ge1$, and let $P:M\to M_r(\mathbb C)$ be a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of constant rank $m$, with $1\le m\le r$. Write $E_P=\{(x,v):P(x)v=v\}$ and give it the projected connection $\nabla s=P\,ds$. For $x\in M$ and $X,Y\in T_xM$, define the curvature two-form with values in $M_r(\mathbb C)$ by

$$F_x(X,Y):=P(x)\bigl(dP_x(X)dP_x(Y)-dP_x(Y)dP_x(X)\bigr)P(x).$$

Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let $V:U\to\mathbb C^{r\times m}$ be a $C^2$ orthonormal frame, meaning $V(x)^*V(x)=I_m$ and $V(x)V(x)^*=P(x)$ for all $x\in U$. Put $A=V^*dV$ and $w=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$, where $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ are the columns of $V$. The induced projected connection on $\det E_P$ has local connection one-form $a=\operatorname{tr}A$ in the unit frame $w$, and its scalar curvature is

$$da=\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)=\operatorname{tr}F.$$

Thus the curvature of the determinant line is the trace of the original bundle curvature, with the same orientation and sign convention.

Assume full AC. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ rank-one orthogonal projection family. Let $E_P$ be its complex line bundle, $\nabla=P\,d$, and $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
For any $C^2$ closed path $\gamma$ subdivided into local unit frames $u_j$, with $A_j=u_j^*du_j$ and transition $u_{j+1}=u_jg_j$ for $g_j$ valued in $U(1)$ at the crossing points, the holonomy is the scalar by which parallel transport acts on its one-dimensional initial fiber. This scalar is the product of the local factors $\exp(-\int_{\gamma_j}A_j)$ and the transition factors $g_j^{-1}$. Thus geometric holonomy includes the frame-transition scalars whenever one frame does not cover the path.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle with $n\geq1$
over a path-connected CW complex $B$ (or over one of the CW-type bases of
[[thm-integral-complex-projective-bundle-theorem]]). By that theorem there are
unique classes $a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)$, $1\leq i\leq n$, such that
$$x_E^{\,n}-a_1x_E^{\,n-1}+a_2x_E^{\,n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^na_n=0\qquad\text{in }H^{2n}(P(E);\mathbb Z),$$
where $x_E\in H^2(P(E);\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of the underlying real
bundle of the tautological line
([[def-complex-projective-bundle-and-tautological-complex-line]]). The
**Chern classes** of $E$ are these coefficients:
$$c_i(E):=a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)\qquad(1\leq i\leq n),$$
completed by the conventions $c_0(E):=1\in H^0(B;\mathbb Z)$ and
$c_i(E):=0$ for $i>n$, and the **total Chern class** is the finite sum
$c(E):=\sum_{i\geq0}c_i(E)=1+c_1(E)+\cdots+c_n(E)\in H^*(B;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-nrqmx-bloch-fiber-model]]. The finite-range operator $H_0$ extends uniquely to a bounded self-adjoint operator $H$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d;\mathbb C^r)$, and $\mathcal F_0$ extends uniquely to a unitary map $\mathcal F:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb T^d_{2\pi};\mathbb C^r)$. For every $k$, $h(k)$ is Hermitian, $\|h(k)\|\le\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|$, and

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc

$$D(a,R)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta-a|<R\}.$$

If $0<r<R$, $|z-a|<r$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, then

$$f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta.$$

derivations.claim: For each fixed $t$ (or for the single projector), [F1] gives the rank-one projector $Q_t=\bigwedge^mP_t$ onto $\det E_{P_t}$. Its image is a complex line bundle over the compact torus, hence is numerable; the torus is a compact smooth CW complex. The determinant-line curvature lemma [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}F_t=\operatorname{tr}(Q_t(dQ_t\wedge dQ_t)Q_t)$ pointwise, with the same orientation convention. Applying [F3] to $Q_t$ proves the displayed equality and integrality, with $c_1$ interpreted by [F5].

For a jointly $C^2$ family, the coefficient function $g(k,t)$ of the two-form $\operatorname{tr}(P_t(dP_t\wedge dP_t)P_t)$ is continuous on the compact set $\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}\times[0,1]$, so it is uniformly continuous. If $t_j\to t$, then $\sup_k|g(k,t_j)-g(k,t)|\to0$; therefore $C(P_{t_j})\to C(P_t)$ by bounding the difference of integrals by the torus's finite area times this supremum. Thus $t\mapsto C(P_t)$ is continuous. Step 1.1 makes it integer-valued, and a continuous integer-valued function on the connected interval $[0,1]$ is constant: otherwise the intermediate-value theorem would give a noninteger value between two distinct integer values. It remains to verify the finite-range clause. The displayed finite sum makes $h(k,t)$ jointly $C^2$ on $\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}\times J$. Ordered eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix depend continuously on its entries: the min-max formula gives $|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|$, by the same Rayleigh-quotient argument as in [F6]. At any $(k_0,t_0)$, choose disjoint small positively oriented circles around the distinct eigenvalues in the selected block of $h(k_0,t_0)$, with their closed disks separated from the complementary eigenvalues. Joint continuity of $h$ and its eigenvalues keeps the selected eigenvalues inside this fixed contour union and the complementary eigenvalues outside on a neighborhood of $(k_0,t_0)$. On the contours, $(zI-h(k,t))^{-1}$ is jointly $C^2$, since matrix inversion is smooth on invertible matrices and the contour remains in the resolvent set. Its contour integral is therefore jointly $C^2$. For completeness, on any component circle $z=c+Re^{it}$ an exterior eigenvalue $\lambda$ has $q=R/|\lambda-c|<1$. The finite geometric identity gives $(z-\lambda)^{-1}=-\sum_{k=0}^N(z-c)^k/(\lambda-c)^{k+1}+r_N(z)$ with $\sup|r_N|\le q^{N+1}/(|\lambda-c|(1-q))$. Each polynomial term has zero circle integral, since $\oint(z-c)^k dz=iR^{k+1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(k+1)t}dt=0$, while the remainder integral has modulus at most $2\pi R\sup|r_N|\to0$. Thus an exterior eigenvalue contributes zero. The interior formula in [F7] and this exterior calculation, applied in a finite orthonormal eigenbasis at each fixed $(k,t)$, give coefficient $1$ on each selected eigenspace and $0$ on its complement. Thus the contour integral is exactly the selected orthogonal projector. The local contour projectors agree on overlaps because they select the same ordered block, so $P(k,t)$ is jointly $C^2$ on the whole product. The general homotopy argument above now applies.

If $V$ is a global $C^2$ periodic orthonormal frame, then $A=V^*dV$ is a globally defined $C^1$ matrix-valued one-form. By [F2] and its proof, $\operatorname{tr}F=d\operatorname{tr}A$ (the trace of $A\wedge A$ vanishes). Hence $C(P)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}d\operatorname{tr}A=0$ by [F4], since the torus has empty boundary.
