derivations.claim: For each integer $m\geq1$, put $U_m:=\{x\in K:|F(x)|<m\}$. These sets are open by continuity of $F$: if $x\in U_m$, continuity gives a neighborhood on which $|F(y)-F(x)|<m-|F(x)|$, hence $|F(y)|<m$. They cover $K$ because every real $|F(x)|$ is less than some positive integer. By the finite-open-cover meaning of compactness in [A2], finitely many $U_{m_1},\ldots,U_{m_k}$ cover $K$, with $k\geq1$ since $K$ is nonempty. Let $M:=\max\{m_1,\ldots,m_k\}$; then $-M<F(x)<M$ for every $x\in K$. Thus $F$ is bounded above and below. This uses the explicitly defined cover and a maximum of finitely many integers, without any simultaneous choice of pointwise neighborhoods. Since $I$ is not identically $+\infty$, choose $x_0\in K$ with $I(x_0)<+\infty$. Therefore $F(x_0)-I(x_0)\leq c\leq\sup_K F<+\infty$, so $c$ is finite. The integrand $e^{nF}$ is bounded above and bounded below by the positive constant $e^{n\inf_KF}$, and $\mu_n$ is a probability measure, hence $0<Z_n<+\infty$ and $\nu_n^F$ is a probability measure.

Let $G\subseteq K$ be open, let $x\in G$ with $I(x)<+\infty$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Continuity of $F$ gives an open neighborhood $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq G$ and $F(y)>F(x)-\varepsilon$ for every $y\in U$. Hence $\int_G e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\geq e^{n(F(x)-\varepsilon)}\mu_n(U)$. By [A1], the logarithm of this integral divided by $n$ has liminf at least $F(x)-\varepsilon-\inf_U I\geq F(x)-\varepsilon-I(x)$. Taking the supremum over finite-rate $x\in G$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the open-set integral lower bound $\liminf_n n^{-1}\ln\int_G e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\geq\sup_{x\in G}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Let $C\subseteq K$ be closed and put $c_C:=\sup_{x\in C}(F(x)-I(x))$, with $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$. If $C=\varnothing$, its integral is zero and the required bound is immediate. Since $F$ is bounded and $I\geq0$, either $c_C$ is finite or $c_C=-\infty$. Suppose first that $c_C$ is finite, and fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $x\in C$ with $I(x)<+\infty$, lower semicontinuity of $I$ and continuity of $F$ give an open neighborhood $V_x$ on which $F\leq F(x)+\varepsilon$ and $I\geq I(x)-\varepsilon$. Choose a ball $U_x$ centered at $x$ with $\overline U_x\subseteq V_x$. For each $x\in C$ with $I(x)=+\infty$, choose $M>\sup_KF-c_C+1$; lower semicontinuity gives an open neighborhood $V_x$ on which $I>M$, and choose such a ball $U_x$. These balls cover compact $C$, so finitely many suffice. Put $C_j:=C\cap\overline U_{x_j}$ for the resulting centers. Each $C_j$ is closed. At a finite-rate center,
$$\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq F(x_j)-I(x_j)+2\varepsilon\leq c_C+2\varepsilon;$$
at an infinite-rate center,
$$\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq\sup_KF-M<c_C-1.$$
The integral over $C$ is bounded by the finite sum $\sum_j e^{n\sup_{C_j}F}\mu_n(C_j)$. Applying [A1] to each closed $C_j$ and using that a finite sum has logarithmic limsup no greater than its largest summand gives
$$\limsup_n\frac1n\ln\int_Ce^{nF}\,d\mu_n\leq c_C+2\varepsilon.$$
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the localized bound in this case. If $c_C=-\infty$, every point of $C$ has infinite $I$. For any real $M$, lower semicontinuity gives, at each $x\in C$, an open neighborhood $V_x$ with $I>M$; choose balls with closures in those neighborhoods and take a finite subcover of $C$. The corresponding closed pieces $C_j$ then satisfy $\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq\sup_KF-M$. The same finite-sum and LDP argument gives a logarithmic limsup at most $\sup_KF-M$. Since $M$ is arbitrary, this limsup is $-\infty=c_C$. Thus in all cases
$$\limsup_n\frac1n\ln\int_Ce^{nF}\,d\mu_n\leq\sup_{x\in C}(F(x)-I(x)).$$

Taking $G=K$ in step 1.2 and $C=K$ in step 1.3 gives $\liminf_n n^{-1}\ln Z_n\geq c$ and $\limsup_n n^{-1}\ln Z_n\leq c$, proving the log-Laplace limit. The function $I_F=I-F+c$ is lower semicontinuous, is nonnegative by the definition of $c$, and has compact sublevel sets because those sets are closed in compact $K$. To prove attainment, set $f:=F-I$, which is upper semicontinuous and bounded above by $\sup_KF$. For every integer $k\geq1$, the set $A_k:=\{x\in K:f(x)\geq c-1/k\}$ is closed and nonempty by the definition of $c$; these sets are nested. Compactness gives $\bigcap_{k\geq1}A_k\ne\varnothing$: otherwise their open complements would cover $K$, and a finite subcover would contradict that a nested finite intersection is nonempty. Every point of this intersection has $f(x)\geq c-1/k$ for all $k$, hence $f(x)\geq c$ and therefore $f(x)=c$. Equality $I_F(x)=0$ holds exactly when $F(x)-I(x)=c$, so its nonempty zero set is precisely the stated maximizing set.

For open $G\subseteq K$, apply the open-set integral lower bound from step 1.2 and subtract the log-normalizer limit in step 2.1. Since $\sup_G(F-I)-c=-\inf_G I_F$, this is the LDP lower bound for $\nu_n^F$.

For closed $C\subseteq K$, apply the closed-set integral upper bound from step 1.3 and subtract the log-normalizer limit in step 2.1. Since $\sup_C(F-I)-c=-\inf_C I_F$, this is the LDP upper bound for $\nu_n^F$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere, using normalized product Haar measure $dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ define $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$. For $t>0$ set

$$\rho_t(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)e_k(x),$$

and at $t=0$ set $\rho_t=\rho_0$ as an almost-everywhere class. For smooth periodic $G$, define

$$P_tG(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat G(k)e_k(x)\quad(t>0),\qquad P_0G:=G.$$

Then on every strip $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $0<\epsilon<T<\infty$, the series for $\rho_t$ and all its space and time derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly; in particular $\rho_t$ is real and smooth for each $t>0$ and $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$. For every finite $T$ and every smooth $G$, $P_tG$ is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$, satisfies $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order there, and $P_tG\to G$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. Moreover

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_tG\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0P_tG\,dx,$$

so $(\rho_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is the unique weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$ in the stated weak formulation. It preserves $0\le\rho_t\le1$ almost everywhere and the mass $\int\rho_t\,dx=\int\rho_0\,dx$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $N\ge3$, $T\ge0$, and let $(\eta_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be the SSEP from the diffusive-model definition. Let $H:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be smooth up to the time endpoints, meaning all time and space derivatives used below extend continuously to $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$. Define

$$F_s^N(\eta):=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_xH(s,x/N),\qquad 0\le s\le T.$$

Then

$$M_t^N:=F_t^N(\eta_t)-F_0^N(\eta_0)-\int_0^t\langle\pi_s^N,\partial_sH(s,\cdot)+\Delta_NH(s,\cdot)\rangle\,ds$$

is a square-integrable martingale, and

$$A_t^N:=N^{2-2d}\int_0^t\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}(\eta_{x+e_i}(s)-\eta_x(s))^2\bigl(H(s,(x+e_i)/N)-H(s,x/N)\bigr)^2\,ds$$

is a continuous predictable increasing process with $(M_t^N)^2-A_t^N$ a martingale. In particular,

$$A_T^N\le T N^{-d}\sum_{i=1}^d\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|\partial_iH(s,\cdot)\|_\infty^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $N\ge3$, $T\ge0$, and let $(\eta_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be the SSEP from the diffusive-model definition with any initial probability vector. For a real smooth periodic $G:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, set

$$M_t^{N,G}:=\langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle-\langle\pi_0^N,G\rangle-\int_0^t\langle\pi_s^N,\Delta_NG\rangle\,ds.$$

Then $M^{N,G}$ is a square-integrable martingale. Its continuous predictable bracket is

$$A_t^{N,G}=N^{2-2d}\int_0^t\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}(\eta_{x+e_i}(s)-\eta_x(s))^2\bigl(G((x+e_i)/N)-G(x/N)\bigr)^2\,ds,$$

in the continuous predictable compensator convention of the finite-chain martingale supplier. In particular,

$$A_T^{N,G}\le T N^{-d}\sum_{i=1}^d\|\partial_iG\|_\infty^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T\ge0$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, and let $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be an increasing family of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\mathcal F$. Let $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a family of real random variables such that each $M_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable, $\mathbb E[M_t^2]<\infty$, $M_0=0$, and $\mathbb E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s$ almost surely for every $0\le s\le t\le T$. Suppose it has càdlàg paths almost surely, meaning there is a measurable event $\Omega_0\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1$ such that, for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$, the path $t\mapsto M_t(\omega)$ is right-continuous on $[0,T)$ and has a finite left limit at every $t\in(0,T]$. Define
$$
D_T=\bigcup_{n\ge0}\{kT/2^n:0\le k\le2^n\},\qquad S_T=\sup_{t\in D_T}|M_t|.
$$
Then $S_T$ is measurable and agrees with the pathwise supremum $\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|$ on $\Omega_0$, and
$$
\mathbb E[S_T^2]\le4\,\mathbb E[|M_T|^2].
$$

derivations.claim: Fix $t\in[0,T]$ and a real-valued smooth periodic $G$. For every $r\ge0$, $P_rG$ is real-valued: since $G$ is real, $\widehat G(-k)=\overline{\widehat G(k)}$, and the Fourier multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2r}$ is real and unchanged by $k\mapsto-k$; pairing the absolutely convergent $k$ and $-k$ terms (with the zero mode real) gives a real sum. By [F2], these functions are smooth, so $H_s=P_{t-s}G$ is an admissible real-valued test in [F3]. Denote its martingale by $M_s^{N,t}$. By [F2], $\partial_sH_s=-\Delta H_s$. The time-dependent martingale identity at its terminal time gives $\langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle=\langle\pi_0^N,P_tG\rangle+M_t^{N,t}+\int_0^t\langle\pi_s^N,(\Delta_N-\Delta)P_{t-s}G\rangle\,ds$, and $M^{N,t}$ starts at zero with terminal second moment equal to the expected bracket.

The fourth spatial derivatives of $P_{t-s}G$ are uniformly bounded for $0\le s\le t$ by [F2]. Taylor's formula for each symmetric second difference therefore gives $\sup_{s,x}|(\Delta_N-\Delta)P_{t-s}G(x)|\le C_{G,T}N^{-2}$. Since $\pi_s^N(\mathbb T^d)\le1$, the drift-error integral in step 1.1 is at most $tC_{G,T}N^{-2}$. By [F3], $\mathbb E_N|M_t^{N,t}|^2\le C'_{G,T}N^{-d}$, so Chebyshev's inequality makes that martingale term tend to zero in probability. Step 1.1 establishes that $P_tG$ is real-valued, and [F2] gives its smoothness; hence the initial-profile assumption applies to this test. Also [F2] gives $\int\rho_0P_tG=\int\rho_tG$. Thus for each fixed $t$, $\langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle\to\int\rho_tG$ in probability.

If $T=0$, the conclusion is the initial-profile assumption. Suppose $T>0$ and fix a finite time mesh $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=T$. Step 2.1 and a finite union bound imply $\max_j|\langle\pi_{t_j}^N,G\rangle-\int\rho_{t_j}G|\to0$ in probability.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus applied twice to each centered second difference, $\|\Delta_NG\|_\infty\le K_G:=\sum_i\|\partial_{ii}G\|_\infty$ for all $N$. The fixed-test martingale in [F4] gives $|\langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle-\langle\pi_s^N,G\rangle|\le K_G|t-s|+2\sup_{0\le u\le T}|M_u^{N,G}|$ for all $s,t\in[0,T]$. By [F4], $\mathbb E|M_T^{N,G}|^2\le T N^{-d}\sum_i\|\partial_iG\|_\infty^2$; [F5] therefore implies $\sup_{u\le T}|M_u^{N,G}|\to0$ in probability. Also [F2] and the mass bound $\int\rho_t\le1$ show $t\mapsto\int\rho_tG$ is Lipschitz with constant $\|\Delta G\|_\infty$. Given $\delta>0$, choose a finite mesh with spacing at most $\delta$; the supremum error is bounded by the maximum mesh error from step 3.1, $2\sup|M^{N,G}|$, and $(K_G+\|\Delta G\|_\infty)\delta$. First let $N\to\infty$ and then $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the stated uniform-in-time convergence in probability.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

derivations.claim: Every supremum defining $M_z$ is measurable because the roots are countable and each $S_y$ has countably many possible finite values. Translation of the common set law and [F2] give $\sum_yP(z\in S_y,|S_y|>u)=\mathbb E[|S_0|\mathbf1_{\{|S_0|>u\}}]$. This tail tends to zero: for example it is at most $u^{-1}\mathbb E|S_0|^2$. The union bound therefore shows $P(M_z>u)\to0$, hence $M_z<\infty$ almost surely. At least $S_z$ contains $z$, and every size is a positive integer, so a finite supremum is attained. Taking the countable union of the null exceptional events proves this simultaneously for all $z$. No independence of the $M_z$ is asserted.

We first prove the assertion for the independent field $X$. Suppose sites are independently marked with probability $r$. If an animal of size at most $m$ contains $k$ distinct marked sites, a depth-first traversal of a spanning tree of that animal, rooted at $0$, visits them in some order using at most $2m$ steps. The successive displacement vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb Z^2$, starting at $0$, have total $\ell^1$ length at most $2m$. There are at most $2^{2k}\binom{2m+2k}{2k}\leq(Cm/k)^{2k}$ such ordered lists for $1\leq k\leq m$: choose signs of their two coordinates and distribute at most $2m$ units among $2k$ nonnegative coordinate magnitudes. Repeated sites and zero coordinates only cause overcounting. For a list of distinct visited sites, all its sites are marked with probability $r^k$. Thus $P(\text{some animal of size at most }m\text{ has }k\text{ marked sites})\leq(C' r m^2/k^2)^k$. This counts marked-site lists rather than all animals and is uniform over all their shapes.

Put $m=2^l$, $r_j=P(X_0\geq2^j)$ and fix $\epsilon=1/4$. Choose a deterministic $a$ such that $C'/a^2\leq e^{-2}$, and a fixed $B\geq2$. For $0\leq j\leq\lfloor\epsilon\log_2m\rfloor$ set $k_j=\lceil\max\{am\sqrt{r_j},B\log m\}\rceil$. If $k_j>m$ the corresponding forbidden event is empty; otherwise step 1.2 bounds its probability by $e^{-2k_j}\leq m^{-2B}$. The union over these $O(\log m)$ values of $j$ is summable along dyadic $m$. For a moment order $Q>2/\epsilon$, the elementary inequality $P(X_0>v)\leq v^{-Q}\mathbb E X_0^Q$ and the fact that every size-at-most-$m$ animal lies in $\Lambda_m=[-m,m]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$ give $P(\max_{\Lambda_m}X_y>m^\epsilon)\leq(2m+1)^2\mathbb E X_0^Q m^{-\epsilon Q}$, also summable in $l$.

If events $E_l$ have summable probabilities, then $P(\bigcup_{l\geq L}E_l)\leq\sum_{l\geq L}P(E_l)\to0$; countable additivity implies that only finitely many $E_l$ occur almost surely. Apply this elementary argument to the failures in step 2.1. Almost surely, for every sufficiently large dyadic $m$, all weights in $\Lambda_m$ are at most $m^\epsilon$, and every size-at-most-$m$ animal has fewer than $k_j$ sites with $X_y\geq2^j$ at each relevant level. The pointwise layer bound $X_y\leq1+\sum_{j\geq0}2^{j+1}\mathbf1_{\{X_y\geq2^j\}}$ then gives, for every animal with $m/2<|\Gamma|\leq m$, $|\Gamma|^{-1}\sum_{y\in\Gamma}X_y\leq1+4a\sum_{j\geq0}2^j\sqrt{r_j}+O(m^{\epsilon-1}\log m)$. Levels above $\epsilon\log_2m$ contribute zero; the error comes from the additive $B\log m+1$ in $k_j$. The constants are deterministic.

A fixed moment order $Q>2$ gives $\sqrt{r_j}\leq(\mathbb E X_0^Q)^{1/2}2^{-Qj/2}$, so the series in step 3.1 converges. Its value is deterministic, and the error tends to zero. Choose $K$ larger than $2+4a\sum_{j\geq0}2^j\sqrt{r_j}$. Every sufficiently large animal belongs to one of the dyadic size ranges in step 3.1. Thus almost surely its average $X$-weight is at most this same $K$, proving the general independent-field assertion.

Apply step 4.1 to $X_y=|S_y|^2$, which is an independent identically distributed field with all moments. Work on the probability-one event where its large-animal bound holds and all $M_z$ are finite. Let $\Gamma$ be any sufficiently large animal, $m=|\Gamma|$, $A=\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z$, and $t=A/(2m)>0$. For each of the finitely many $z\in\Gamma$ with $M_z>t$, choose a root $y(z)$ attaining its maximum; to avoid even a selection convention take the first such root in a fixed enumeration of $\mathbb Z^2$. Let $Y$ be the distinct chosen roots, $s_y=|S_y|$, $U=\sum_{y\in Y}s_y^2$, and $V=\sum_{y\in Y}s_y$. Low-weight sites contribute at most $A/2$, and at most $s_y$ sites can be assigned to a given $S_y$. Hence $U\geq A/2=mt$. Since $s_y>t$ for chosen roots, $V\leq U/t$.

The set $\Delta=\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{y\in Y}S_y$ is a finite connected animal containing every root in $Y$, because every chosen set meets $\Gamma$ and is connected. Its size is at least $m$ and at most $m+V$. Therefore the same large-animal bound gives $U\leq\sum_{y\in\Delta}|S_y|^2\leq K|\Delta|\leq K(m+U/t)$. If $t>2K$, this would imply $U<2Km$ while step 5.1 gives $U\geq mt>2Km$, a contradiction. Thus $t\leq2K$ and $A\leq4Km$. Taking the deterministic constant $K_0=4K$ proves the envelope assertion uniformly over every sufficiently large animal. Only the given probability laws and countable additivity were used, without constructing any new infinite family.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\geq1$, let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^n$, and let $\rho$ be a positive-definite Hermitian matrix, meaning $\langle\rho v,v\rangle>0$ for each nonzero $v\in\mathcal H$, with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Write $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}=M_n(\mathbb C)$ with inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(Y^*X)$, linear in the first argument, and let $M_n(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$ by left multiplication. For $\Omega=\rho^{1/2}$, the standard modular data are
$$JX=X^*,\qquad \Delta X=\rho X\rho^{-1},\qquad \sigma_t(A)=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}\quad(A\in M_n(\mathbb C),\ t\in\mathbb R).$$
The vector state of $\Omega$ is $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$. If $H=H^*$ has energy unit joules, $\beta>0$ has unit joules$^{-1}$, $\hbar>0$ has unit joule-seconds, and $\rho=e^{-\beta H}/Z$ with $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$, then the physical-time dynamics
$$\alpha_s(A)=e^{isH/\hbar}Ae^{-isH/\hbar}\quad(s\text{ in seconds})$$
satisfies
$$\alpha_s=\sigma_{-s/(\beta\hbar)}.$$
On the finite-dimensional C$^*$-algebra $M_n(\mathbb C)$, $\omega$ is a $\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in the physical-time convention of the stated KMS definition, with strip width $\beta\hbar$ seconds. If $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, then $k_B$ has units joules per kelvin and $T$ has units kelvins.

derivations.claim: Since $\rho^{it}=\operatorname{diag}(p^{it},(1-p)^{it})$, conjugating $E_{12}$ multiplies it by $p^{it}(1-p)^{-it}=e^{it\log(p/(1-p))}$. Thus the modular parameter has coefficient $\log(p/(1-p))$, which is dimensionless.

If $\rho=e^{-\beta H}/Z$ with $H=\operatorname{diag}(E_1,E_2)$, then $p/(1-p)=e^{-\beta(E_1-E_2)}$ because the common partition function cancels. Hence $\log(p/(1-p))=-\beta(E_1-E_2)$, and substituting $t=-s/(\beta\hbar)$ yields $e^{is(E_1-E_2)/\hbar}$. The energy gap alone gives no time frequency until $\hbar$ is specified, and the state alone gives no energy gap until $H$ and $\beta$ are specified.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.
For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If $Y$ is Banach,
then $\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is Banach for the operator norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $\Lambda:C(K,\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ be real-linear, positive in the sense that $f\ge0$ implies $\Lambda(f)\ge0$, and normalized by $\Lambda(1)=1$. Then there is a Borel probability $\mu$ on $K$ with $\Lambda(f)=\int_K f\,d\mu$ for every continuous real $f$. It is outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets by compact subsets. No Dependent Choice is required.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

derivations.claim: Positivity gives $\|(I+K)x\|\ge\|x\|$ on $D(K)$, by pairing $(I+K)x$ with $x$. Its range is closed: if $(I+K)x_n$ converges, the bound makes $x_n$ Cauchy, and $Kx_n=(I+K)x_n-x_n$ converges, so closedness in [F1] identifies the limit in $D(K)$. The range has zero orthogonal complement because $\ker(I+K)^*=\ker(I+K)=0$; [F1] makes the closed range all of $\mathcal H$. Thus $B=(I+K)^{-1}$ exists, $\|B\|\le1$, $\ker B=0$ and $\operatorname{ran}B=D(K)$ is dense. For $x=(I+K)u$ and $y=(I+K)v$, symmetry gives $\langle Bx,y\rangle=\langle x,By\rangle$, while $\langle Bx,x\rangle=\|u\|^2+\langle Ku,u\rangle\ge0$. Hence $B$ is a positive self-adjoint contraction and $KB=I-B$.

We shall use uniqueness of finite complex measures on $[0,1]$ from their continuous integrals. If their difference $
u$ integrates every continuous function to zero, then for any relatively open $O\subseteq[0,1]$ the continuous functions $f_n(b)=\min(1,n\operatorname{dist}(b,[0,1]\setminus O))$ increase to $\mathbf1_O$; take $f_n=1$ when $O=[0,1]$. Dominated convergence against its finite total variation gives $
u(O)=0$. Since also $
u([0,1])=0$, the sets where $
u$ vanishes form a lambda-system. The relatively open sets form a generating pi-system, so [F6] proves $
u=0$ on all Borel sets. This also applies to any finite linear combination of positive measures.

Scalar Laplace uniqueness will identify the evolution. If a bounded continuous $h:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$ satisfies $\int_0^\infty e^{-zt}h(t)\,dt=0$ for every real $z>0$, apply [F7] to the $C^1$ diffeomorphism $t\mapsto s=e^{-t}$ from $(0,\infty)$ to $(0,1)$, with inverse $-\log s$ and absolute Jacobian $e^{-t}=s$, and take $z=n+1$. The endpoints have Lebesgue measure zero; boundedness of $h$ makes the complex integrands absolutely integrable. Then $\int_0^1s^n h(-\log s)\,ds=0$ for all integers $n\ge0$, with any value assigned at $s=0$. Polynomial approximation [F3] implies the same equality against every continuous test on $[0,1]$. If $h(t_0)\ne0$, multiplication by a constant complex phase and continuity give a time interval on which its real part is strictly positive. A nonnegative continuous piecewise-linear hat supported inside the corresponding interval of $s$ has strictly positive integral against that real part, contradicting the preceding test identity. For $t_0=0$ use a one-sided time neighborhood and a smaller interior interval. Therefore $h=0$.

Fix a dense sequence in $\mathcal H$ and let $P_n$ be the projection onto the span of its first $n$ terms. Finite Gram–Schmidt, skipping zero remainders and using positive real normalizations, constructs these projections deterministically, and density gives $P_nx\to x$ for every $x$. The compression $B_n=P_nBP_n$ is a positive contraction on that finite-dimensional span and zero on its complement. For every complex polynomial $p$, diagonalize the compression using [F2], with eigenvalues $b_j\in[0,1]$. For $x=\sum_j c_j e_j+x_\perp$ its squared image norm is $\sum_j|p(b_j)|^2|c_j|^2+|p(0)|^2\|x_\perp\|^2\le(\sup_{0\le b\le1}|p(b)|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus $\|p(B_n)\|\le\sup_{0\le b\le1}|p(b)|$, including the zero complement. Boundedness and strong convergence $B_n\to B$ imply $p(B_n)x\to p(B)x$ by induction on powers. Hence the same norm bound holds for $p(B)$. By [F3], polynomial approximations define $f(B)$ for every $f\in C([0,1];\mathbb C)$, independently of the approximation, with $\|f(B)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$. Norm limits preserve sums, products, the identity and conjugate adjoints. If $f\ge0$, approximating its continuous square root gives $f(B)=\sqrt f(B)^*\sqrt f(B)\ge0$. This constructs the required continuous calculus without a spectral theorem.

For $z>0$ the strong improper integral $R_zx=\int_0^\infty e^{-zt}U_tx\,dt$ exists. The identity $\|U_tx-U_sx\|=\|(U_{t-s}-I)x\|$ and strong continuity at zero give uniform norm-continuity of the orbit, and the scalar exponential factor is uniformly continuous on each finite interval by its bounded derivative. Hence on a finite interval the integrand is uniformly norm-continuous, so uniform-mesh Riemann sums are Cauchy in $\mathcal H$; their tails have norm at most $e^{-zT}\|x\|/z$. Thus $R_z$ is bounded by $1/z$. The group law makes $U_tD(K)=D(K)$ and $KU_tx=U_tKx$ by difference quotients. For $x\in D(K)$ the same Riemann sums converge also after applying $K$, and closedness gives differentiation/integration in its graph. The continuous-curve fundamental theorem [F7], followed by the exponentially small endpoint limit, applied to $(e^{-zt}U_tx)'=e^{-zt}(iK-z)U_tx$ yields $(z-iK)R_zx=x$. The estimate $\|(z-iK)x\|^2=z^2\|x\|^2+\|Kx\|^2$, closedness and the zero kernel of the adjoint $z+iK$ show that $z-iK$ is onto with inverse norm at most $1/z$, just as in step 1.1. Density extends $R_z=(z-iK)^{-1}$ to every $x$.

For $x
e0$, the real functional $f\mapsto\langle f(B)x,xangle/\|x\|^2$ is positive and normalized. Apply [F4] on $[0,1]$ and multiply its probability measure by $\|x\|^2$, obtaining a positive measure $
u_x$; set $
u_0=0$. Its continuous integrals are $\langle f(B)x,xangle$, first for real $f$, then for complex $f$ by linearity. Define $$
u_{x,y}= rac14\sum_{j=0}^3 i^j
u_{x+i^j y}.$$ Polarization gives $\int f\,d

For every Borel $D$, the form $(x,y)\mapsto
u_{x,y}(D)$ is positive sesquilinear. Expanding its nonnegative value on $x+cy$, and minimizing over $c\in\mathbb C$ (with the zero-diagonal case treated by arbitrary large multiples), gives $|

For continuous $f,h$, multiplicativity of the calculus gives $$\int h\,d
u_{f(B)x,y}=\langle h(B)f(B)x,yangle=\int hf\,d
u_{x,y}.$$ Step 1.2 implies $d
u_{f(B)x,y}=f\,d
u_{x,y}$ as measures. Conjugate symmetry yields $d
u_{f(B)x}=|f|^2d
u_x$; in particular $$\|f(B)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d
u_x.$$ These identities use only continuous factors and scalar measures, not a postulated Borel operator calculus.

Since $
u_{Bz}(\{0\})=0$ by step 4.2, step 4.1 makes its mixed measure with any vector zero on $\{0\}$. Hence $
u_x(\{0\})=
u_{x-Bz}(\{0\})\le\|x-Bz\|^2$. The dense range from step 1.1 allows this upper bound to be arbitrarily small, proving $
u_x(\{0\})=0$ and then $
u_{x,y}(\{0\})=0$ for all $x,y$. Thus no zero-endpoint mass is hidden by the reciprocal change of variable below.

If a real $b_0$ is in the resolvent of $B$, let $L=(B-b_0)^{-1}$. For every positive integer $n$, step 4.2 with $x=L^nz$ gives $d
u_z=|b-b_0|^{2n}d
u_{L^nz}$. Thus on $|b-b_0|<\varepsilon$, $$
u_z(\{|b-b_0|<\varepsilon\})\le(\varepsilon\|L\|)^{2n}\|z\|^2.$$ Choose $\varepsilon\|L\|<1$ and let $n	o\infty$. The neighborhood is null for every diagonal measure and therefore for every mixed measure by step 4.1. The real resolvent set is open by the inverse Neumann series. It is covered by the rational intervals contained in these null neighborhoods; this is a subfamily of a fixed countable base. Countable subadditivity proves that all $
u_{x,y}$ are carried by $\sigma(B)\cap[0,1]$.

The identity in step 4.2 makes $(B^nx)$ Cauchy: for $n,m\ge N$ its squared difference is at most $4\int_{[0,1)}b^{2N}d
u_x$, which tends to zero by [F5]. Let its limit be $Px$. Again $\|(B-I)B^nx\|^2=\int(1-b)^2b^{2n}d
u_x	o0$, so $Px\in\ker(I-B)$. For $y$ in this kernel, self-adjointness gives $\langle B^nx,yangle=\langle x,yangle$, and therefore $x-Px$ is orthogonal to the kernel. Thus $P$ is its orthogonal projection by [F1]. This kernel equals $\ker K$, since $KB=I-B$. Dominated convergence in $\langle B^nx,yangle=\int b^n d
u_{x,y}$ gives $
u_{x,y}(\{1\})=\langle P_0x,yangle$.

On $(0,1]$ put $\lambda(b)=b^{-1}-1$ and define $g_{x,y}(t)=\int e^{it\lambda(b)}d\nu_{x,y}(b)$, omitting the null endpoint by step 5.1. It is bounded and continuous by dominated convergence and step 4.1. For $z>0$, scalar Fubini, applied to the finite positive measures in the polarization formula, gives its Laplace transform as $\int (z-i\lambda(b))^{-1}d\nu_{x,y}(b)$. The reciprocal is the continuous function $$r_z(b)=\frac{b}{zb-i(1-b)},\qquad r_z(0)=0.$$ By step 2.1, $r_z(B)=B(zB-i(I-B))^{-1}$, and $KB=I-B$ shows $(z-iK)r_z(B)=I$ on $\mathcal H$. Step 2.2 identifies this with $R_z$. Thus $g_{x,y}$ and $\langle U_tx,y\rangle$ have equal Laplace transforms. Step 1.3 gives equality for $t\ge0$; conjugate symmetry and $U_{-t}=U_t^*$ give it for negative $t$ as well.

Push $\nu_{x,y}|_{(0,1]}$ forward by $\lambda$ to obtain $\mu_{x,y}$. Positivity, total mass, sesquilinearity and the variation bound pass to the pushforward. If $E\ge0$ is in the resolvent of $K$ and $b_0=(1+E)^{-1}$, the bounded inverse identity $$(B-b_0)^{-1}=-(1+E)I-(1+E)^2(K-E)^{-1}$$ follows by multiplying on $D(K)=\operatorname{ran}B$. Therefore $b_0$ is in the resolvent of $B$. Step 5.2 and the homeomorphism $(0,1]\to[0,\infty)$ show that the pushed measures are carried by $\sigma(K)$. Their atom at $E=0$ is the atom at $b=1$, computed in step 5.3. All these statements include vectors in the ground subspace and the possibility that the excited subspace is zero.

Step 6.1 proves the Fourier pairing formula, and step 6.2 proves the remaining measure properties. For $Q=I-P_0$, its measures have zero atom at zero by that formula for the atom and are carried by $\sigma(K)$; the stated gap therefore places them in $[g,\infty)$. Let $Q\in\{2,3,4\}$ and let $L\geq1$ be an integer. The finite Potts-clock space is
$$\mathcal H_{Q,L}:=(\mathbb C^Q)^{\otimes L}$$
of dimension $Q^L$, with the tensor-product Hermitian inner product taken linear in its first argument and computational orthonormal basis
$$|a_1,\ldots,a_L\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_L\rangle,\qquad a_j\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}.$$
On $\mathbb C^Q$, this inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}x_a\overline{y_a}$, and on elementary tensors it is $\langle u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_L,v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_L\rangle=\prod_{j=1}^L\langle u_j,v_j\rangle$.
For a unit vector $u$, the notation $|u\rangle\langle u|$ denotes the endomorphism $v\mapsto\langle v,u\rangle u$. On one site use the clock and shift convention
$$R_Q|a\rangle=e^{2\pi i a/Q}|a\rangle,\qquad M_Q|a\rangle=|a-1\!\!\pmod Q\rangle.$$
Set $|+\rangle:=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|a\rangle$. For $1\leq j\leq L$, let $P_j$ be $|+\rangle\langle+|$ on factor $j$ and identity on every other factor. For $1\leq j<L$, let
$$D_{j,j+1}:=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|aa\rangle\langle aa|$$
act on factors $j,j+1$ and as identity on the others. The open-chain local operators are
$$e_{2j-1}:=\sqrt Q\,P_j\quad(1\leq j\leq L),\qquad e_{2j}:=\sqrt Q\,D_{j,j+1}\quad(1\leq j<L).$$
Equivalently, these are the exact clock-shift operators of the open Potts representation: $e_{2j-1}=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}M_{Q,j}^{\,r}$ and $e_{2j}=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}R_{Q,j}^{\,r}R_{Q,j+1}^{-r}$. Thus there are $2L-1$ operators and no bond from site $L$ back to site $1$.

For real coefficients $J_1,\ldots,J_{2L-1}$, define the weighted open-chain matrix
$$H_{Q,L}(\mathbf J):=-\sum_{i=1}^{2L-1}J_i e_i.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $Q\in\{2,3,4\}$ and let $L\geq1$ be an integer. The finite Potts-clock space is
$$\mathcal H_{Q,L}:=(\mathbb C^Q)^{\otimes L}$$
with its standard tensor-product Hermitian inner product and computational orthonormal basis
$$|a_1,\ldots,a_L\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_L\rangle,\qquad a_j\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}.$$
On one site use the clock and shift convention
$$R_Q|a\rangle=e^{2\pi i a/Q}|a\rangle,\qquad M_Q|a\rangle=|a-1\!\!\pmod Q\rangle.$$
Set $|+\rangle:=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|a\rangle$. For $1\leq j\leq L$, let $P_j$ be $|+\rangle\langle+|$ on factor $j$ and identity on every other factor. For $1\leq j<L$, let
$$D_{j,j+1}:=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|aa\rangle\langle aa|$$
act on factors $j,j+1$ and as identity on the others. The open-chain Temperley-Lieb operators are
$$e_{2j-1}:=\sqrt Q\,P_j\quad(1\leq j\leq L),\qquad e_{2j}:=\sqrt Q\,D_{j,j+1}\quad(1\leq j<L).$$
Equivalently, these are the exact clock-shift operators of the open Potts representation: $e_{2j-1}=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}M_{Q,j}^{\,r}$ and $e_{2j}=Q^{-1/2}\sum_{r=0}^{Q-1}R_{Q,j}^{\,r}R_{Q,j+1}^{-r}$. Thus there are $2L-1$ operators and no bond from site $L$ back to site $1$.

For real coefficients $J_1,\ldots,J_{2L-1}$, define the weighted open-chain matrix
$$H_{Q,L}(\mathbf J):=-\sum_{i=1}^{2L-1}J_i e_i.$$
For a self-adjoint finite matrix $H_{Q,L}$ and real $\beta$, let $\Lambda(H_{Q,L})$ be its finite set of distinct eigenvalues and let $\Pi_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace. Define
$$B_\beta(H_{Q,L}):=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda(H_{Q,L})}e^{-\beta\lambda}\Pi_\lambda,\qquad Z_\beta:=\operatorname{tr}B_\beta(H_{Q,L}),\qquad \rho_\beta:=Z_\beta^{-1}B_\beta(H_{Q,L})$$
whenever $Z_\beta>0$. Here a density matrix means a self-adjoint positive semidefinite endomorphism of trace one. The A-page Gibbs lemma establishes that the displayed $H_{Q,L}$ is self-adjoint and that $Z_\beta>0$ for every finite real $\beta$.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Use a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(\mathcal M,g)$ without boundary, of signature $(-+++)$. Global hyperbolicity means strong causality and compact causal diamonds $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, where $J^\pm$ are defined by consistently directed causal curves; strong causality means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods that each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W_2$ on $\mathcal M\times\mathcal M$ satisfying $P_xW_2=P_yW_2=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W_2)=\mathcal C_g^+$, the positive-frequency null relation whose pairs $(x,\xi;y,-\eta)$ have nonzero future-null covectors $\xi,\eta$ equal to a common positive multiple of the metric-dual tangent of one affinely parametrized future null geodesic at the two endpoints, with covector parallel transport and either endpoint parameter order; coincident endpoints have $\eta=\xi$. The manifold is the smooth domain on which this free-field model is posed; no singular interior is included.

Assume that after a smooth Cauchy surface $\Sigma_0$ (a spacelike hypersurface met exactly once by each inextendible causal curve of the modeled region), the modeled future exterior is exactly the Schwarzschild exterior of fixed mass $M$, with areal radius $r>r_s$, $r_s=2GM/c^2$, and metric
$$ds^2=-\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dt^2+\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2+r^2(d\vartheta^2+\sin^2\vartheta\,d\varphi^2).$$
Here $t$ is the stationary Schwarzschild time in seconds, $r$ is in metres, and $\vartheta,\varphi$ are the usual dimensionless angular coordinates. The metric is a fixed background: the field does not change it. The retarded coordinate is $u=t-r_*/c$, where $r_*=r+r_s\log(r/r_s-1)$. The associated geometric surface-gravity parameter in inverse metres and its time-frequency version are, by this model's normalization,
$$\kappa_{\rm geom}:=\frac{1}{2r_s}=\frac{c^2}{4GM},\qquad k:=c\kappa_{\rm geom}=\frac{c^3}{4GM}>0.$$

Adopt one real, linear, massless, minimally coupled scalar field on $(\mathcal M,g)$. Its smooth classical solutions are $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathcal M;\mathbb R)$ satisfying $P\phi=0$ for $P:=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b$, where $\nabla$ is the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$; the canonical scalar field has length degree $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Adopt its bosonic Fock quantization, with smeared field operators $\Phi(f)$ for $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathcal M;\mathbb R)$, where the pairing uses the metric volume density $d{\rm vol}_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3|$, and the algebra generated by those smeared fields. A state $\varpi$ is a positive normalized linear functional on that algebra, and its two-point distribution is $W_2(f,g)=\varpi(\Phi(f)\Phi(g))$. Require $W_2$ to be a Hadamard bisolution for $P$. This free-field equation and quantization are adopted, not derived from collapse matter. In the incoming asymptotic modes at past null infinity $\mathscr I^-$, the state is the ground state: its incoming positive-frequency modes have zero occupation. Here $\mathscr I^-$ and future null infinity $\mathscr I^+$ denote the asymptotic endpoints of incoming and outgoing null rays in the asymptotically flat region.

For each outgoing retarded-time coordinate $u$, measured in seconds, adopt the increasing null-ray label
$$U(u)=U_H-Ae^{-ku},\qquad U_H\in\mathbb R\ {\rm seconds},\quad A>0\ {\rm seconds}.$$
The two-point current channel for this label is exactly the tested exponential channel defined by the ray map above. It is the time-coordinate version of the reduced exponential-current branch, whose length flow parameter is $u_{\rm geom}=cu$, inverse-length parameter is $\kappa_{\rm geom}=k/c$, and detailed-balance convention is the same. The identification of the four-dimensional near-horizon packet channel with this one-dimensional tested current is an adopted model premise, not a restriction theorem for a four-dimensional field. The separate accelerated-detector and two-state-rate branch is not part of this collapse model.

For a spherical-harmonic angular index $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$, measured in radians per second (radians are dimensionless), let $\Gamma_\ell(\omega)\in[0,1]$ be the dimensionless transmission probability supplied by the stationary radial-scattering model. Assume $\Gamma_\ell$ is continuous on every compact frequency interval $K=[\omega_-,\omega_+]\subset(0,\infty)$ with $\omega_-<\omega_+$. By definition in this model, the normalized near-horizon signal mode $a_{\ell,\omega}$ and independent incoming vacuum mode $e_{\ell,\omega}$ are mapped to the outgoing mode $b_{\ell,\omega}$ and its complementary mode $d_{\ell,\omega}$ by
$$\begin{pmatrix}b_{\ell,\omega}\\d_{\ell,\omega}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}&\sqrt{1-\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}\\-\sqrt{1-\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}&\sqrt{\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{\ell,\omega}\\e_{\ell,\omega}\end{pmatrix}.$$
All four mode operators use the unit one-particle normalization of the supplied channel, so their occupations are dimensionless. The squared coefficient $\Gamma_\ell(\omega)$ is the transmitted fraction; no transmission coefficient is calculated here.

In the adopted frequency-diagonal Fock interpretation, the positive-frequency Fourier coefficient of the ordered current two-point function is $\omega/2$ times the mode occupation. Thus the occupation associated with spectral coefficient $S_k(\omega)$ is, by this model's normalization, $2S_k(\omega)/\omega$ for $\omega>0$. This identification is part of the adopted channel model; it is not a detector response or an observed particle count.

For each compact frequency interval $K=[\omega_-,\omega_+]\subset(0,\infty)$ with $\omega_-<\omega_+$, the normalized packet space is $\mathcal H_K=L^2(K,d\omega)$. A packet is a smooth compactly supported $f:K\to\mathbb C$ with $\int_K|f(\omega)|^2d\omega=1$; $f$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{1/2}$. Its outgoing number form at retarded-time center $s$ is
$$B_{\ell,s}(f,g):=\varpi\!\left(a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f)^*a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(g)\right),$$
where $a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f)$ is the annihilation operator of that normalized packet translated to center $s$ at $\mathscr I^+$, and $s$ is measured in seconds. Adopt the scattering and local-decay assumption that for each fixed $K$, these bounded sesquilinear forms converge in operator norm as $s\to+\infty$ to the direct integral of the exponential near-horizon channel and the independent incoming vacuum channel mixed by the displayed passive map. Explicitly, operator-norm convergence means
$$\sup_{\|f\|_2,\|g\|_2\le1}|B_{\ell,s}(f,g)-B_{\ell,\infty}(f,g)|\longrightarrow0.$$
No uniform error rate over bands, angular indices, or packet families is assumed.

Only after this late-time convergence is fixed may a stationary-frequency limit be taken. For each $\omega_0$ in the interior of such an interval $K$, use a specified family $f_\epsilon\in\mathcal H_K$ with common compact support $K$, $\|f_\epsilon\|_2=1$, and spectral probability measures $|f_\epsilon(\omega)|^2d\omega$ converging weakly to the point mass $\delta_{\omega_0}$. This is concentration of normalized packets, not $L^2$-norm convergence to a non-normalizable monochromatic mode.

In the channel defined above, let $s=u-v$ and let $\omega$ be angular frequency in seconds$^{-1}$. Its two-point distribution in centered time is
$$C_k(s)=-\frac{k^2}{16\pi}\operatorname{csch}^2\left(\frac{k}{2}(s-i0)\right).$$
Its Fourier spectrum, using $\widehat C_k(\omega)=\int_{\mathbb R}C_k(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds$ in the distributional sense, is
$$S_k(\omega)=\frac{\omega}{2(e^{2\pi\omega/k}-1)}\quad(\omega\ne0),\qquad S_k(0)=\frac{k}{4\pi}.$$
Thus the precise detailed-balance relation at strip width $\theta=2\pi/k$ seconds is $S_k(-\omega)=e^{\theta\omega}S_k(\omega)$ for every $\omega>0$. No measured temperature is assigned.

Separately, for each fixed $\omega>0$, give $\mathbb C$ the second-variable-linear Hilbert inner product $\langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C}=\bar z w$, so $1\in\mathbb C$ is a unit vector, and put $\mathcal F=\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C)$. Write $|m\rangle$ for the normalized vector in its $m$-particle sector, with $|0\rangle=\Omega$; the annihilation map satisfies $a_{\mathbb C}(1)|m\rangle=\sqrt m\,|m-1\rangle$ on finite-particle vectors. Its maximal closed domain is
$$D(a_{\mathbb C}(1))=\left\{\sum_{m\ge0}\psi_m|m\rangle:\sum_{m\ge0}m|\psi_m|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Let $\Gamma:(0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ be any pointwise transmissivity function; no measurability is needed because every assertion below is mode-by-mode. Every square root below denotes the unique nonnegative real square root, which exists for each nonnegative argument in the usual Dedekind-complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. Let $\mathcal H=\mathcal F\widehat\otimes\mathcal F$ with product basis $|m,n\rangle=|m\rangle\otimes|n\rangle$. The tensor-factor annihilation operators $a=a_{\mathbb C}(1)\otimes I$ and $e=I\otimes a_{\mathbb C}(1)$ act on basis vectors by $a|m,n\rangle=\sqrt m\,|m-1,n\rangle$ and $e|m,n\rangle=\sqrt n\,|m,n-1\rangle$, with a zero result when the corresponding index is zero, and have domains
$$D(a)=\left\{\sum_{m,n\ge0}c_{mn}|m,n\rangle:\sum_{m,n\ge0}m|c_{mn}|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(e)=\left\{\sum_{m,n\ge0}c_{mn}|m,n\rangle:\sum_{m,n\ge0}n|c_{mn}|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
On their common domain $D:=D(a)\cap D(e)$ define, for each $\omega$, the two output operators by the following linear transformation, with $D(b_\omega)=D(d_\omega)=D$:
$$b_\omega=\sqrt{\Gamma(\omega)}\,a+\sqrt{1-\Gamma(\omega)}\,e.$$
The complementary output is $d_\omega=-\sqrt{1-\Gamma(\omega)}\,a+\sqrt{\Gamma(\omega)}\,e$, also defined on $D$. Let $\mathscr D_{\rm fin}=\operatorname{span}\{|m,n\rangle:m,n\in\mathbb N_0\}$ be the algebraic finite-particle subspace. It is contained in $D$ and invariant under $a,e$ and their creation operators; on it define $b_\omega^\dagger=\sqrt{\Gamma(\omega)}\,a^\dagger+\sqrt{1-\Gamma(\omega)}\,e^\dagger$ and $d_\omega^\dagger=-\sqrt{1-\Gamma(\omega)}\,a^\dagger+\sqrt{\Gamma(\omega)}\,e^\dagger$ as the corresponding creation combinations. Let $\psi_\omega\in D(a_{\mathbb C}(1))$ be a normalized signal vector and put the environment in its unit vacuum vector $\Omega_e=|0\rangle$. Then $\Psi_\omega:=\psi_\omega\otimes\Omega_e$ lies in $D$: if $\psi_\omega=\sum_m\psi_m|m\rangle$, the $a$-domain sum is $\sum_m m|\psi_m|^2<\infty$ and the $e$-domain sum is zero. Put $n_\omega=\|a_{\mathbb C}(1)\psi_\omega\|^2<\infty$ and define the output occupation by the quadratic form $\mathfrak n_{\rm out}(\omega):=\|b_\omega\Psi_\omega\|^2$. Then $\mathfrak n_{\rm out}(\omega)=\Gamma(\omega)n_\omega$. For the Planck occupation function $n_\theta(\omega)=(\exp(\theta\omega)-1)^{-1}$ with width $\theta>0$ measured in seconds, one has $n_\theta(\omega)>0$ for every $\omega>0$. Consequently, a filter preserving this same width at every positive frequency must satisfy $\Gamma(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=n_\theta(\omega)$ and hence $\Gamma(\omega)=1$ at every $\omega$. Frequency-dependent filtering can nevertheless preserve Planck form at another width: $\Gamma_*(\omega)=(\exp(\theta\omega)+1)^{-1}$ lies in $(0,1)$ and varies with $\omega$, while $\Gamma_*(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=n_{2\theta}(\omega)$. This is an algebraic channel statement; it does not identify $\Gamma$ with a four-dimensional black-hole scattering coefficient.

For the Planck occupation function $n_\theta(\omega)=(\exp(\theta\omega)-1)^{-1}$ with width $\theta>0$ measured in seconds, one has $n_\theta(\omega)>0$ for every $\omega>0$. Consequently, a filter preserving this same width at every positive frequency must satisfy $\Gamma(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=n_\theta(\omega)$ and hence $\Gamma(\omega)=1$ at every $\omega$. Frequency-dependent filtering can nevertheless preserve Planck form at another width: $\Gamma_*(\omega)=(\exp(\theta\omega)+1)^{-1}$ lies in $(0,1)$ and varies with $\omega$, while $\Gamma_*(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=n_{2\theta}(\omega)$. This is an algebraic channel statement; it does not identify $\Gamma$ with a four-dimensional black-hole scattering coefficient.

Adopt SI units. Let $c>0$ have units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $G>0$ have units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\hbar>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,s}$, and $k_B>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mass $M>0$ is a fixed model parameter in kilograms. Use a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(\mathcal M,g)$ without boundary, of signature $(-+++)$. Global hyperbolicity means strong causality and compact causal diamonds $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, where $J^\pm$ are defined by consistently directed causal curves; strong causality means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods that each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W_2$ on $\mathcal M\times\mathcal M$ satisfying $P_xW_2=P_yW_2=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W_2)=\mathcal C_g^+$, the positive-frequency null relation whose pairs $(x,\xi;y,-\eta)$ have nonzero future-null covectors $\xi,\eta$ equal to a common positive multiple of the metric-dual tangent of one affinely parametrized future null geodesic at the two endpoints, with covector parallel transport and either endpoint parameter order; coincident endpoints have $\eta=\xi$. Here $t$ is the stationary Schwarzschild time in seconds, $r$ is in metres, and $\vartheta,\varphi$ are the usual dimensionless angular coordinates. The metric is a fixed background: the field does not change it. The retarded coordinate is $u=t-r_*/c$, where $r_*=r+r_s\log(r/r_s-1)$. A state $\varpi$ is a positive normalized linear functional on that algebra, and its two-point distribution is $W_2(f,g)=\varpi(\Phi(f)\Phi(g))$. Require $W_2$ to be a Hadamard bisolution for $P$. This free-field equation and quantization are adopted, not derived from collapse matter. In the incoming asymptotic modes at past null infinity $\mathscr I^-$, the state is the ground state: its incoming positive-frequency modes have zero occupation. Here $\mathscr I^-$ and future null infinity $\mathscr I^+$ denote the asymptotic endpoints of incoming and outgoing null rays in the asymptotically flat region.

For each outgoing retarded-time coordinate $u$, measured in seconds, adopt the increasing null-ray label
$$U(u)=U_H-Ae^{-ku},\qquad U_H\in\mathbb R\ {\rm seconds},\quad A>0\ {\rm seconds}.$$
The two-point current channel for this label is exactly the tested exponential channel defined by the ray map above. It is the time-coordinate version of the reduced exponential-current branch, whose length flow parameter is $u_{\rm geom}=cu$, inverse-length parameter is $\kappa_{\rm geom}=k/c$, and detailed-balance convention is the same. derivations.claim: Fix $\ell$ and a normalized $f$ supported in $K$. The postulate identifies the near-horizon occupation with $2S_k(\omega)/\omega$; by [F1] and $\theta=2\pi/k$, this is $n_\theta(\omega)$. Work with the joint incoming number quadratic form supplied by the direct-integral Fock channel in [A2]. Write $q_K$ for its conjugate-linear-first, linear-second polarization on $\mathcal H_K\oplus\mathcal H_K$, with the first summand the signal and the second the incoming vacuum; its diagonal is the adopted input occupation. The frequency-diagonal signal form is $q_K((g,0),(h,0))=\int_K\overline{g(\omega)}h(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)d\omega$. It is bounded, since $n_\theta$ is continuous and bounded on the compact positive-frequency band $K$. The vacuum condition gives $q_K((0,h),(0,h))=0$. These are the quadratic-moment data of the two input channels already adopted in [A2]; they require neither a pure signal vector nor a normal density-matrix representation, and no assertion that a monochromatic annihilator belongs to the compactly smeared field algebra is used. To see that there is no additional cross-moment assumption, put $F=(g,0)$ and $E=(0,h)$. Positivity and sesquilinearity give $0\le q_K(F+zE,F+zE)=q_K(F,F)+2\operatorname{Re}(zq_K(F,E))$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$. Unless $q_K(F,E)=0$, a suitable phase and arbitrarily large modulus of $z$ make this negative. Hence both cross pairings vanish. In quadratic-moment Hilbert-space language, quotienting the input form by its null vectors and completing sends every vacuum annihilation label $E$ to the zero vector; its pairing with every finite signal annihilation image is therefore zero. Thus all cross pairings are fixed by positivity, with no operator product-domain or extra finite-cross-moment axiom. The passive map in [A2], with the same real coefficients as [F2], sends the output packet label to $J_\ell f=(\sqrt{\Gamma_\ell}\,f,\sqrt{1-\Gamma_\ell}\,f)$. The coefficients are bounded measurable functions on $K$, so $J_\ell$ is defined on $\mathcal H_K$ and $\|J_\ell f\|^2=\|f\|^2$. Pulling back the adopted input number form gives $B_{\ell,\infty}(f,f)=q_K(J_\ell f,J_\ell f)=\int_K|f(\omega)|^2\Gamma_\ell(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)d\omega$. This calculates the diagonal of the adopted packet form directly, rather than treating $b^*b$ as an unbounded operator on an unspecified domain or extending [F2]'s vector theorem by assertion.

Operator-norm convergence in [A2] implies $|B_{\ell,s}(f,f)-B_{\ell,\infty}(f,f)|\le\|B_{\ell,s}-B_{\ell,\infty}\|\|f\|_2^2\to0$; using $\|f\|_2=1$ and the value computed in step 1.1 proves the finite-packet limit.

Set $g(\omega)=\Gamma_\ell(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)$ and $d\mu_\epsilon=|f_\epsilon(\omega)|^2d\omega$. The common band $K$ is compact and bounded away from zero, and [F3] gives $n_\theta(\omega)>0$ there; with the postulated continuous $\Gamma_\ell$, $g$ is bounded and continuous on $K$. For any $\eta>0$, continuity gives a neighborhood $V$ of $\omega_0$ in $K$ on which $|g(\omega)-g(\omega_0)|<\eta$. Choose a continuous $q:K\to[0,1]$ with $q(\omega_0)=0$ and $q=1$ outside $V$. Weak convergence $\mu_\epsilon\rightharpoonup\delta_{\omega_0}$ gives $\int q\,d\mu_\epsilon\to0$, hence $\mu_\epsilon(K\setminus V)\to0$. Therefore $\left|\int_Kg\,d\mu_\epsilon-g(\omega_0)\right|\le\eta+2\|g\|_\infty\mu_\epsilon(K\setminus V)\to\eta$; as $\eta$ is arbitrary, the integral tends to $g(\omega_0)$.

Apply step 2.1 at each fixed $\epsilon$, then step 2.2 to the resulting spectral integral. This order yields $\Gamma_\ell(\omega_0)/(e^{2\pi\omega_0/k}-1)$ and does not replace a finite-width integral by its central-frequency value.

By the definition of $T_\infty$ in the Statement, $\theta\omega=\hbar\omega/(k_BT_\infty)$ for every $\omega>0$; solving $\theta=2\pi/k$ gives $T_\infty=\hbar k/(2\pi k_B)$. Substituting the model value $k=c^3/(4GM)$ from [F4] gives $T_\infty=\hbar c^3/(8\pi GMk_B)$. Its units are $(\mathrm{J\,s})(\mathrm{s^{-1}})/(\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})=\mathrm K$. The conclusion is a model-derived spectral parameter and contains no observed temperature.
